detail.abstract: This paper draws on a real life case from an IT department of a German University to compare and contrast the enactment of two distinct methods of requirement elicitation in the context of a specific service design initiative. The objective of this paper is to contrast and compare two methods, a traditional Focus Group and an adapted Lego Serious Play, in order to gain novel insights into the process of collaborative ideation. The findings demonstrated remarkable differences between the two types of sessions with respect to engagement, creativity and collaborative behaviour. The findings further suggested reframing of the requirement elicitation towards being embodied, power-laden and affective processes. Such a reframing was primarily due to the role of Lego bricks that materialized anew the process of collective ideation. New forms of human-Lego otherness reconfigured the collaborative boundaries and afforded a more democratic and an existentially safer context for creative engagements, constructing ideas, generating and sharing new knowledge. The paper also offers practical guidelines for novel ways to design and cultivate contexts for learning and innovation.

title: Layered Agentic Retrieval: A Publishing Architecture for Agent-Native Web Surfaces

detail.title: Layered Agentic Retrieval: A Publishing Architecture for Agent-Native Web Surfaces

detail.abstract:
As AI agents transition from read-only assistants to autonomous actors, the human-readable web is failing them. Current retrofitting approaches, such as schema.org-enhanced HTML or Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), force agents to parse unstructured or weakly-structured corpora or expend finite token budgets on human-centric rendering pipelines. In response, a parallel publishing layer is taking shape: major AI operators — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Stripe, and Google — are increasingly exposing machine-legible surfaces optimized for autonomous traversal, deterministic retrieval, and reduced token consumption. This paper identifies and analyzes this emerging publishing pattern as Layered Agentic Retrieval (LAR).

LAR is a publisher-side architectural commitment to surface deterministic, machine-legible data designed explicitly for agent traversal. We articulate LAR's three core commitments — plain-text substrates, progressive disclosure, and workflow-organized hierarchies — and situate it within the lineages of RESTful hypermedia and the Semantic Web. By delineating the limits of current retrofitting approaches, this paper establishes LAR as a dedicated institutional layer through which publishers can expose machine-legible retrieval, policy, and operational surfaces to autonomous agents — the structural artifact onto which cryptographic attestation attaches and on which emerging legal provenance frameworks can operate.

title: Algorithmic Dramaturgy: A Sociotechnical Mode of Platform-mediated Service Performance
affiliations: TalTech and Bentley University - Information and Process Management

detail.title: Algorithmic Dramaturgy: A Sociotechnical Mode of Platform-mediated Service Performance
detail.abstract: Ridehailing constitutes a digitally orchestrated performance where algorithms act as invisible directors. Drivers engage in dual-audience impression management, performing for both customers and algorithms, while customers alternate between audience, co-performer, and evaluator. The result is re- composed service performance: authenticity, autonomy, and quality are redefined by platform logics. Classical service-as-theatre (SaT) and algorithmic management (AM) each capture partial truths: the former explains the “how” of performance, the latter the “why” of compliance. Smiles, politeness, and composure remain—not as pre-digital traces, but as human resonance adapted to algorithmic orchestration. By bridging AM and SaT, in this short paper, we offer an empirical study and preliminary theorization of algorithmic dramaturgy (AD)–a sociotechnical mode of service performance in which human and algorithmic actors co-produce relational order. We advance theoretical conversations about sociotechnical control and service work at the intersection of SaT and AM, extending service relation research in the digital age.

title: The System's Shadow: How AI Persona Alters Arousal, Behavior, and Workplace Performance Beyond What Users Report
affiliations: Kozminski University, Kozminski University, , Quinnipiac University, Kozminski University and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: The System's Shadow: How AI Persona Alters Arousal, Behavior, and Workplace Performance Beyond What Users Report

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study protocol was approved by the Internal Research Ethics Board Committee at Kozminski University, Poland.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Polish National Science Center (NCN) OPUS 21 grant no. 2021/41/B/HS4/03664.

detail.abstract: As AI systems become embedded in workplace workflows, their interactional style-the persona they present-may function as an ambient condition shaping cognition, affect, and performance. We tested this in a controlled experiment (N = 58) where participants completed a marketing collaboration task supervised by one of two AI chatbot personas grounded in leadership theory: a supportive Servant Leader and an antagonistic Dark Triad leader. Combining self-report questionnaires, continuous psychophysiological recording (electrodermal activity and facial electromyography), LLMassisted behavioral coding, and blind expert-rated performance, we examined whether persona reliably shifts outcomes across measurement modalities. Results revealed a striking multi-level pattern. The Dark Triad persona produced significantly elevated sympathetic arousal (72% higher peak electrodermal amplitude), a tenfold increase in behavioral resistance, substantially greater strategy diversity and switching, fourfold more jailbreaking attempts with qualitatively more aggressive strategies, and significantly lower expert-rated work quality (d = 0.71-0.83). Yet retrospective self-reports of enjoyment, satisfaction, and focused attention showed no significant between-group differences. Equivalence testing clarified this dissociation as graded: self-report effects were bounded below d = 0.75 but could not be established as equivalent at d = 0.50. Of fourteen hypotheses, eight were supported and two partially supported, with confirmation tracking measurement modality: behavioral, autonomic, and performance hypotheses were overwhelmingly confirmed; self-report and somatic physiological hypotheses were not. These findings reframe AI persona as a causal design dimension with consequences for well-being, performance, and human-AI collaboration, warning that organizations relying solely on satisfaction surveys risk underestimating the costs of poorly calibrated interactional design.

title: Generative AI and the Reorganization of Labor Demand
affiliations: Purdue University - Daniels School of Business, Purdue University - Daniels School of Business and

detail.title: Generative AI and the Reorganization of Labor Demand
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to transform work, but less is known about how firms reorganize labor demand as the technology diffuses. Existing research has largely focused on which occupations are exposed to AI or whether exposed jobs decline. We extend this debate by examining whether firms adjust by changing where they hire, what jobs contain, or both. Using a nationwide dataset of job postings in the United States, covering all sectors of the economy, we construct a dynamic, posting-level measure of generative AI exposure with a two-stage large language model pipeline. The pipeline identifies the tasks described in each posting and classifies the extent to which generative AI can perform or assist them. We then decompose changes in aggregate exposure into two margins: reallocation of demand across jobs and redesign of tasks within jobs. We document three main findings. First, generative AI exposure is dynamic rather than fixed, changing substantially over time. Second, labor demand adjusts through both margins. Hiring reallocation explains the largest share of the aggregate decline in exposure, accounting for 52% on average, while within-job redesign becomes increasingly important, accounting for 39.5%. A complementary Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition shows that shifts in occupational composition account for about 90% of the exposure change attributable to observable job characteristics. Third, adjustment differs across the job ladder. Senior jobs adjust earlier and mainly through reallocation, whereas junior jobs adjust through a broader mix of reallocation, redesign, and their interaction. These findings suggest that labor-market adjustment to generative AI is a process of organizational reconfiguration, in which firms reshape both hiring demand and the task architecture of work.

title: Non-personal Data in the European Union: Law, Governance and Justifications

detail.title: Non-personal Data in the European Union: Law, Governance and Justifications
detail.abstract:
The file includes chapters 3, 4 and 6 from my forthcoming monograph 'Non-personal Data in the European Union: Law, Governance and Justifications' (Cambridge University Press 2027) (forthcoming).

Chapter 3: Theories of Data Governance. This chapter examines the theoretical and conceptual accounts that shape competing models for governing non-personal data. It canvasses the various political-philosophical perspectives that provide justifications for how non-personal data ought to be regulated in society. This sheer theoretical plurality is made up of libertarian, liberal-egalitarian, communitarian, welfarist, institutionalist, republican, critical and relational-egalitarian frameworks of data governance. In short these accounts conceptualise data in various ways using different metaphorical objects and foreground diverse sets of actors and institutions for governing data. Each theory is assessed for its explanatory power and its implications for understanding 'unilateral data control'. By mapping these competing accounts, the chapter highlights that data governance can be shaped by different theoretical and conceptual perspectives and show contested normative commitments.

Chapter 4: EU Data Law and Non-personal Data. This chapter examines EU data law as a legal domain that aims to govern non-personal data mainly through a 'market instrumental' lens. In doing so, it essentially views non-personal data as a tradeable commodity to be exchanged in markets. EU data law is made up of two main frameworks: vertical and horizontal. The vertical framework includes sector-specific rules (eg finance and chemicals) as well as in EU competition law, platform law, consumer law and AI law. The horizontal framework, which is comprised of the Free Flow of Data Regulation, the Data Governance Act (DGA) and the Data Act, is geared towards building fairness and weaker parties' participation in data markets. The chapter also touches on the Common European Data Spaces, the Data Union Strategy and the Digital Omnibus Regulation proposal. Ultimately it is argued that while EU data law seeks to empower 'weaker' market actors, its heavy reliance on market-friendly justifications often sidelines thicker forms of social justice.

Chapter 6: Just Data Law and Governance: Core Components and Principles. This chapter proposes a framework for just data law and governance in the EU, moving beyond the current market instrumentalism that characterises the existing legal framework on non-personal data. To address injustices in data law and governance, it argues in favour of an approach grounded in concurrent strategies. First, it advocates for principles to drive down unilateral control, namely the numerus clausus of intellectual property rights and the social function of IP. Second, it calls for a shift towards enabling control seekers to make an actual, meaningful choice in contracts to prevent data control holders from leveraging superior bargaining power. Finally, the chapter outlines four pillars for framing non-personal data as a commons: democratic participation and deliberation to decide what gets datafied; access rules; use limitations based on processing purposes; more equitable value distribution among a broader range of actors, such as urban communities and SMEs. The core components of just data law reconcile different theoretical worldviews with practical governance tools to foster a more equitable data future.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the market position of artificial intelligence (AI) within an adoption life cycle, responding to the practical question of whether AI is still emerging, scaling, maturing, or already entering renewal. Rather than treating AI as a single homogeneous technology, the paper develops a cross-sector synthesis that distinguishes between adoption breadth, deployment depth, lifecycle governance, and adaptive maturity. Evidence from recent adoption surveys and AIindex reports indicates that AI use has become widespread across organizations and households, but enterprise-wide scaling and measurable value capture remain uneven. Accordingly, the paper argues that AI, as a broad market, is best classified as in late growth and scaling, moving into early lifecycle integration and governance. However, specific AI applications occupy different stages of maturity: digital twins, predictive analytics, and process automation are closer to maturity in selected sectors, while agentic AI and frontier generative AI remain closer to experimentation or early growth, despite rapidly growing attention. A five-stage AI adoption life cycle is proposed: design and experimentation; growth and scaling; lifecycle integration and governance; maturity and adaptive intelligence; and reconfiguration or renewal. The paper concludes that the most scientifically defensible answer is conditional: AI is no longer merely introductory, but it is not uniformly mature. Its present position is a distributed, sector-dependent transition from growth to governance-supported maturity.

title: The BI Gap: From Business Intelligence to Governed AI-enabled Decision Capability

detail.title: The BI Gap: From Business Intelligence to Governed AI-enabled Decision Capability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this report is a conceptual and practice-oriented synthesis and did not involve human participants, personal data, clinical data, surveys, interviews, or experiments.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this report.

detail.abstract:
This Executive Research Report develops the BI Gap as a governance problem in the transition from governed Business Intelligence to AI-enabled decision capability. It argues that Business Intelligence remains a necessary information foundation for management control, but becomes insufficient once AI systems influence interpretation, prioritisation, escalation, workflow participation or bounded action.

The report introduces Decision Governance as a decision-point framework for AI-enabled BI, FP&A, controlling and management-control contexts. The framework specifies what AI may observe, classify, prioritise, recommend, prepare, escalate or execute; where AI must stop; which tools it may access; who remains accountable; how behaviour is monitored; and what evidence must remain auditable.

The report synthesises research streams on Business Intelligence and analytics, management control systems, AI governance, human-AI collaboration and agentic information systems. Its central proposition is that the governance object shifts from trusted information to AI-mediated participation in decision execution as organisations move from BI-supported visibility toward Analytical AI, Generative AI and, where appropriate, bounded agentic participation.

The report is an evidence-informed conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical validation study, maturity model or implementation standard. Its contribution is to translate the BI Gap and Decision Governance logic into a practice-oriented governance-learning framework for FP&A, controlling and management-control contexts, including a 90-day governance-learning cycle before scale.

The report further argues that AI capability awareness and AI literacy are governance prerequisites. Without sufficient understanding of Analytical AI, Generative AI and Agentic AI, managers, controllers and FP&A professionals may underestimate both the opportunity and the accountability risks of AI-mediated decision work.

title: PAARA Connector-DPIA Methodology: A Privacy-Aware Risk Assessment Model for Enterprise GenAI Connectors

detail.title: PAARA Connector-DPIA Methodology: A Privacy-Aware Risk Assessment Model for Enterprise GenAI Connectors
detail.abstract:
Enterprise generative AI tools operate through connector integrations OAuth scopes, Microsoft Graph permissions, REST API bridges, and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines  that link large language models to enterprise data sources including email, document repositories, HR systems, finance platforms, and customer databases. Major data protection authorities have published guidance on AI and privacy obligations, but current guidance provides limited operational treatment of connector-layer retrieval governance as a distinct assessment object. Every existing Data Protection Impact Assessment framework frames its analysis around the AI model or product. The integration layer — the OAuth scope, the permission, the retrieval boundary, the prompt-injection vector, the insider-accessible data surface — is treated as an undifferentiated subset of generic information-security controls.

This paper introduces the PAARA Connector-DPIA Methodology: a six-component practitioner model for assessing enterprise AI connectors as privacy-relevant and security-relevant processing enablers. The methodology provides a connector inventory framework, WP29 nine-criteria analysis at the connector layer, an OAuth and Graph permission risk register, a retrieval-boundary and prompt-injection threat model, an insider-risk amplification assessment, and a cross-framework alignment table spanning GDPR Article 35, EU AI Act Article 27, ISO/IEC 42005:2025, NIST AI 600-1, OWASP LLM Top 10, and related standards. A worked example and practitioner checklist are included. The methodology is designed to be executable by DPOs, CISOs, and privacy engineers, and submittable to regulatory bodies as a practitioner framework contribution.

title: PAARA-Agentic: Connector and Tool Governance for Agentic AI Systems

detail.title: PAARA-Agentic: Connector and Tool Governance for Agentic AI Systems
detail.abstract: Enterprise agentic AI systems — including multi-agent orchestrators built on Model Context Protocol server architectures, Microsoft 365 Copilot agentic workflows, and enterprise AI agents with tool-calling capability — do not merely retrieve and surface enterprise data. They act. This paper introduces PAARA-Agentic, a governance methodology extending the PAARA Connector-DPIA Methodology to assess connector, tool, MCP server, and agent-identity risks in enterprise agentic AI deployments. Four new assessment components address action-authority risk, agent identity and delegation governance, multi-agent interaction risk, and human oversight adequacy. A three-tier MCP server certification model — Approved, Restricted, Prohibited — operationalises regulatory recommendations from Spain's AEPD (18 February 2026) and Singapore's IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (January 2026). Three verified NVD entries (CVE-2025-32711, CVE-2025-6514, CVE-2025-53967) confirm the risk surface addressed is active in production deployments. The methodology maps to NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, ISO/IEC 42005:2025, and the community draft NIST Agentic AI Profile.

title: Efficiency and Satisfaction of a Queuing Kiosk System in a Private Higher Education Institution

detail.title: Efficiency and Satisfaction of a Queuing Kiosk System in a Private Higher Education Institution
detail.abstract: The study employed a quantitative research design using survey questionnaires to measure the efficiency and user satisfaction of the queuing kiosk system at a private higher education institution in San Jose City, Nueva Ecija. Among the major aspects evaluated were the waiting period, delivery speed, ease of use, and user satisfaction. The questionnaire was administered to 150 students, who served as the final respondents in the study. Data gathered from the respondents were tallied and analyzed using descriptive statistics. Findings revealed that the queuing kiosk system has proved to efficient, having succeeded in eliminating waiting times, increasing speed, and creating an easy-to-use interface. A high satisfaction rate shows that the technology has succeeded in creating positive experiences for students. Thus, the system provides a valuable technological tool to enhance the effectiveness of administration and to provide services to students.

title: Comparative Analysis of Business Models: Creating a Need vs. Identifying a Need in the Online Tertiary Sector
affiliations: University of Burdwan

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of Business Models: Creating a Need vs. Identifying a Need in the Online Tertiary Sector
detail.abstract: Products and services offered by companies can broadly be categorized into two types: those that create a consumer need and those that identify and fulfill an existing need. This study aims to evaluate which of these business approaches tends to result in greater success. To achieve this, the paper undertakes a comparative analysis of multiple business dimensions, including marketing strategies, associated risks, net income or losses, and consumer behaviour.

title: People vs. Content on Social Media: A Choice for Policy

detail.title: People vs. Content on Social Media: A Choice for Policy
detail.abstract: Informatization brings about great advances in scientific and economic development. We have witnessed how the Internet and the Web 2.0 model disrupted centralized media production by enabling individual contributors to compete on an equal footing. Eventually, however, social media platforms developed proprietary algorithms to control what content users see, with a view to maximizing time spent on the platform and, consequently, their own ad revenue. It is highly likely that such "informational traps" tip social homeostasis towards polarization, attention deficit, and potentially the spread of populism. Here we propose a recommendation system promoting the least frequent posters to negate online activism. In real systems a responsible user should be allowed to dial between the present engagement-centric algorithm and the proposed coverage-centric alternative. We suggest the need for a policy akin to the GDPR that would require the platforms to offer such choice.

title: From Desktop EDI to Hybrid Mobile APIs: Modernizing B2B E-Commerce Supply Chains for Real-Time Operational Visibility

detail.title: From Desktop EDI to Hybrid Mobile APIs: Modernizing B2B E-Commerce Supply Chains for Real-Time Operational Visibility
detail.abstract: As corporate environments increasingly demand real-time agility, legacy Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) systems-the traditional backbone of Business-to-Business (B2B) e-commerce-have introduced severe operational bottlenecks due to their rigid, desktop-bound, batch-processing constraints. This paper investigates the strategic, technological, and operational paradigms of migrating from legacy EDI architectures to real-time, hybrid mobile Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). Utilizing a qualitative multiple case study approach, this study analyzes two enterprise supply chains that successfully constructed a decoupled middleware API gateway over their existing EDI infrastructure. Grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the findings reveal that a hybrid bridge model eliminates data latency-reducing transaction visibility cycles from hours to less than 2.5 seconds-and drives a 34% reduction in warehouse operational cycle times by empowering decentralized field workers with mobile enterprise tools. Ultimately, this paper provides an empirical strategic model for e-commerce executives looking to execute a mobile-first B2B transformation while seamlessly maintaining backend compliance with global trading partners.

title: EQUITY-GRC: A Quantitative Framework for Gender-Responsive Cybersecurity Governance — Proposing the Equity-Adjusted Governance Risk Score (EGRS), Cognitive Diversity Latency Model, and Shadow AI Leadership Metric

detail.title: EQUITY-GRC: A Quantitative Framework for Gender-Responsive Cybersecurity Governance — Proposing the Equity-Adjusted Governance Risk Score (EGRS), Cognitive Diversity Latency Model, and Shadow AI Leadership Metric

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. This research was conducted independently with no external funding, institutional affiliation, or organisational sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as independent research by the author.

detail.abstract: No existing cybersecurity governance standard provides a mechanism to quantify, price, or remediate gender representation gaps in governance teams as a computable organisational risk. This paper proposes the EQUITY-GRC Framework: a nine-pillar governance standard that embeds gender equity as a measurable, auditable, and financially quantified cybersecurity risk variable operating within COBIT 2019 and NIST SP 800-53 without modification of either standard. The framework introduces three original instruments. The Equity-Adjusted Governance Risk Score (EGRS) is a composite index of six Key Risk Indicators with defined threshold-triggered governance actions within COBIT APO12 and NIST RA-3. The Cognitive Diversity Latency (CDL) Model is a theoretical calibration model — grounded in collective intelligence research (Woolley et al., 2010) — that converts governance team homogeneity into a dollar cost per incident. The Shadow AI Leadership Metric (SALM) proposes a governance control filling a documented normative gap in ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and NIST AI RMF GOVERN 3.1 regarding who should govern AI risk detection. The framework is anchored in verified data from the Bangladesh fintech sector. All three instruments are presented as proposed models requiring empirical validation through organisational pilot data. Pilot partners are invited.

publicationDetails.detailsText: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series No. 2026-06

detail.abstract: Firms in the digital economy often pay little tax in the countries where their customers are based. In response, market countries have introduced digital service taxes on the revenue of these firms to indirectly tax their profits. We study the incidence of these taxes using data on Amazon, the largest online retailer. We find that in most countries, Amazon increased its fees by roughly the amount of the digital service tax. Firms using Amazon as a platform have largely passed these increased fees on to consumers. Large digital firms thus bear only a small part of the tax burden, but the tax may nevertheless succeed in making them less competitive relative to brick-and-mortar retailers.

title: Trademark Law as Regulation of Expression: Why Article 10 ECHR Should Become the Internal Grammar of European Trademark Law

detail.title: Trademark Law as Regulation of Expression: Why Article 10 ECHR Should Become the Internal Grammar of European Trademark Law
detail.abstract:
This chapter argues that European trademark law increasingly operates as a system of expression regulation and should therefore be reconstructed in light of Article 10 ECHR. Trademark law no longer merely protects consumers against deception: through anti-dilution protection, expansive infringement standards, and morality-based registration rules, it increasingly governs the circulation of cultural and political meanings attached to trademarks, which themselves have become communicative resources used in parody, artistic appropriation, political criticism, activism, journalism, and public debate.

The chapter first identifies the two principal contexts in which these tensions arise: restrictions on expressive reuse of trademarks and refusals to register allegedly immoral or offensive signs. It then analyses the Article 10 principles most relevant to trademark law, focusing on the listener-oriented structure of freedom of expression and its implications for confusion-based and anti-dilution protection; the constitutional treatment of commercial speech and the dangers of overly broad conceptions of “commerciality”; the heightened protection afforded to speech on matters of public interest; the protection of artistic expression, satire, and humour; the broader tolerance required for criticism of powerful corporate actors; and the contextual protection of offensive or provocative expression. Building on this framework, the chapter argues that freedom of expression should not remain an external defence applied only after infringement has been established. Instead, Article 10 values should shape trademark doctrine internally, including the interpretation of use in the course of trade, use in relation to goods or services, anti-dilution protection, due cause, and morality or public-order exclusions. It concludes that trademark law can retain its legitimate market-regulating role only if Article 10 ECHR becomes part of its internal doctrinal structure.

title: Competing Visions of the Corporation and Fiduciary Obligation: Some Comparative Law Perspectives
affiliations: Monash University - Faculty of Law and Monash University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Competing Visions of the Corporation and Fiduciary Obligation: Some Comparative Law Perspectives

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 934/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Corporate law has periodically been declared moribund or intellectually exhausted, most notably in Bayless Manning’s influential assessment of mid-twentieth-century scholarship. Contrary to such predictions, however, the field experienced a resurgence from the 1980s onward, driven by the emergence of new theoretical frameworks, including agency theory, communitarianism, team production theory, and convergence debates. Among these, agency theory, as advanced via the law and economics movement, achieved dominance. By recasting the corporation as a nexus of contracts, this contractarian movement narrowed the focus of corporate law to the mitigation of agency costs between managers and shareholders. Contractarianism, while analytically powerful, contributed to the marginalization of fiduciary law and attenuated the moral and social dimensions traditionally associated with corporate governance.

This article revisits these developments through the lens of Professor Deborah DeMott’s scholarship, which offers a sustained critique of law and economics orthodoxy. DeMott reconceptualizes fiduciary obligation as a historically grounded, equitable doctrine that operates not merely as a set of contractual duties but as a flexible, situation-specific mechanism for ensuring accountability and regulating power. Her work highlights the enduring normative and societal functions of fiduciary law and challenges the reductionist tendencies of contractarianism. Building on this insight, the article situates DeMott’s analysis within a comparative framework, contrasting Delaware corporate law with contemporary developments in the United Kingdom and Australia. In doing so, the article highlights alternative trajectories in corporate theory and fiduciary obligation that preserve a broader conception of the corporation’s social role.

title: The Agentic Governance Ribbon: A Provenance-first Framework for Governing Agentic AI across Regulatory Regimes
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University - Heinz College

detail.title: The Agentic Governance Ribbon: A Provenance-first Framework for Governing Agentic AI across Regulatory Regimes
detail.abstract:
Existing AI governance frameworks-NIST AI RMF 1.0, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the EU AI Act, and the major commercial governance platforms built around them-were architected primarily for predictive and generative AI systems. They govern what models say. They have comparatively little to say about what agentic systems do: the autonomous actions, tool calls, and runtime-evolving behaviour that distinguish agents from prior generations of AI. This paper introduces the Agentic Governance Ribbon (AI-GR), a provenance-first governance framework designed to close that framework-level gap. 

AI-GR organises governance as a 5×3 matrix-five lifecycle gates (Conceive, Build, Deploy, Operate, Evolve) crossed with three risk tiers (Critical, High, Managed). Each cell of the matrix emits a Governance Provenance Record (GPR): a content-addressable, cryptographically attested, append-only entry that captures the decision, the evidence, the approving authority, and the applicable regulatory regimes. GPR entries chain together through linkage pointers, producing a tamper-evident provenance sequence in which the chain-rather than any individual document-is the audit artifact. 

The framework is vendor-neutral, designed to sit on top of existing governance infrastructure (IBM watsonx.governance, AWS and Azure model cards, Credo AI, MOSS, OVERT, NIST AI 600-1 documentation) rather than replace it. A single GPR entry can simultaneously satisfy the evidence demands of seventeen regulatory regimes spanning AI-specific, sectoral, and jurisdictional law. An open-source reference implementation in Python (Apache 2.0) ships alongside this paper, with three worked examples covering clinical decision support, agentic financial advice, and AI-augmented software engineering. 

AI-GR is offered as a contribution to the practitioner and research community rather than as a commercial product. The author makes no claim to having empirically validated the framework at production scale; the present paper is a framework-and-design contribution, with empirical evaluation reserved for future work as adoption emerges.

detail.title: Heterogeneity, Tokenization, and Wealth Dynamics in the Digital Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper No. 05/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong Institute for Monetary & Financial Research (HKIMR) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper is written by Lin William Cong (Nanyang Technological University) and Zhiheng He (Renmin University of China).

We provide an overview of the growing literature on tokenization, digital platforms, and the macroeconomics of programmable value. We then contribute by building a continuous‑time model of user heterogeneity, platform growth, and wealth dynamics to analyze how digital and on‑chain economies co‑evolve. Tokenization enables real‑time capitalization of network effects, accelerating adoption but producing non‑ergodic wealth distributions that amplify inequality among participants. We further incorporate fiat‑linked digital payment media—including stablecoins and central bank digital currencies—to explore how their introduction affects platform liquidity and wealth dynamics. These fiat‑based instruments act as stabilizing counterparts to endogenous platform tokens, mitigating volatility and speculative feedback loops. The analysis highlights how heterogeneous adoption, endogenous liquidity creation, and cross‑platform substitution jointly shape inequality, platform life cycle, and financial stability. Overall, the paper provides not only a structured synthesis of tokenomics studies but also a unified theoretical framework for understanding wealth dynamics and inequality under the coexistence of private and sovereign digital monies and payment systems.

title: MSME Pulse: A Satellite-Augmented Machine Learning Framework for Predicting MSME Financial Distress in India's Informal Economy
affiliations: Bennett University

detail.title: MSME Pulse: A Satellite-Augmented Machine Learning Framework for Predicting MSME Financial Distress in India's Informal Economy
detail.abstract: India's 63 million micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) contribute over 30% of GDP and employ approximately 400 million workers, yet remain virtually invisible to conventional financial surveillance infrastructure. This paper introduces MSME Pulse, a predictive analytics framework that forecasts MSME financial distress 4-9 months before detection by traditional non-performing asset (NPA) indicators. The system fuses four previously uncombined data streams: NASA VIIRS nighttime light satellite imagery, Ministry of Corporate Affairs MCA21 company filing signals, GST compliance delay proxies, and district-level macroeconomic indicators. A two-stage ensemble model combining XGBoost gradient boosting with engineered temporal features achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.9853 on held-out 2024 data, with an average distress detection lead time of 6.8 months across 678 validated NPA events. The framework covers 50+ Indian districts across 8 MSME sectors and produces district-level stress probability scores updated monthly. Results suggest that nighttime light intensity decline and company strike-off rates are the strongest leading indicators of MSME credit stress, preceding NPA events by 5-8 months. Policy implications for RBI, SIDBI, and NBFCs are discussed.

title: Collateral Damage: The Political Economy of State Fragmentation and Socioeconomic Collapse in War-Torn Sudan
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Collateral Damage: The Political Economy of State Fragmentation and Socioeconomic Collapse in War-Torn Sudan

detail.abstract: The civil war in Sudan (April 2023-present) has caused one of the most severe national economic collapses of the twenty-first century. By late 2025, real GDP had contracted by more than 40 percent from prewar levels, extreme poverty surged from 33 percent to 71 percent of the population, unemployment reached 47 percent, and inflation exceeded 170 percent. Over 14 million people have been displaced, more than 19 million children are out of school, and nearly half the population faces acute food insecurity. This paper examines the causal relationship between political instability and economic deterioration using vector autoregression (VAR), Granger causality tests, and lagged correlation analysis on annual data from 2018 to 2026. The central finding is that political shocks-particularly coups and conflict intensity-Granger-cause economic contraction with a one-to two-year lag (*r* =-0.89 for conflict intensity → GDP growth). The paper integrates three theoretical frameworks: (1) the youth bulge hypothesis (Sudan's total fertility rate of 4.32, youth dependency ratio of 78.1, and 40.7% of the population under age 14 created a recruitment pool for armed groups); (2) the resource curse (gold smuggling, estimated at 23-36.8 billionin lost revenues over the past decade, finances both warring parties and reduces incentives for peace); and (3)state fragility theory (historical institutional weakness, originating from the 1989 Islamist coup, converted the war into a self-perpetuating conflict trap). Recovery to pre-conflict GDP levels is unlikely before 2031, requiring reconstruction costs estimated at 23-36.8 billion in lost revenues over the past decade, finances both warring parties and reduces incentives for peace; and (3)state fragility theory (historical institutional weakness, originating from the 1989 Islamist coup, converted the war into a self-perpetuating conflict trap). Recovery to pre-conflict GDP levels is unlikely before 2031, requiring reconstruction costs estimated at 0.5-1 trillion. The paper concludes that durable peace demands demilitarizing the economy, suppressing the parallel gold trade, and creating mass youth employment-not merely a cessation of hostilities.

title: Pricing Life Insurance Using Bivariate Temperature-Mortality Seasonal Hidden Markov Models
affiliations: Université Laval, Université Laval and Université Laval

detail.title: Pricing Life Insurance Using Bivariate Temperature-Mortality Seasonal Hidden Markov Models
detail.abstract: We study the dependence between weekly mortality and temperature through a non-homogeneous Seasonal Hidden Markov Model (SHMM) with trend. The framework jointly models mortality and temperature while allowing for regime switches, explicit seasonality, smooth longterm trends, and time-varying transition probabilities in latent dynamics. We show that the general identifiability and strong consistency results of Touron (2018) apply to our Poissonand Gaussian-emission specifications. We estimate the model on weekly Italian mortality and temperature data using two-and three-state specifications. Empirically, the SHMM improves fit relative to non-switching benchmarks and yields an interpretable state-dependent characterization of the temperature-mortality relationship. We then develop a change-of-measure framework for pricing mortality-linked insurance contracts that incorporates temperature-related mortality risk and latent regime uncertainty.

title: Comparative Assessment of Case Definitions on the Epidemiology of Asymptomatic Pulmonary Tuberculosis in China: A Nationwide Surveillance Analysis, 2021–2024

detail.abstract:
Background:  The proportion and epidemiological profile of asymptomatic tuberculosis (TB) vary widely depending on symptom criteria, yet no standardized case definition exists. Understanding how definitional differences impact surveillance estimates and risk factor associations is critical for accurate burden assessment and targeted intervention. This study compares two common symptom-based definitions of asymptomatic TB and evaluates their influence on estimated prevalence, risk factor associations, temporal trends, and geographic distribution in China.

Methods: We analyzed national TB surveillance data (January 2021–December 2024, n=1,037,934). Asymptomatic TB was defined as: D1: absence of all TB-related symptoms; D2: absence of cough, expectoration, or hemoptysis. We compared case proportions (McNemar’s test), assessed risk factors (logistic regression), and analyzed temporal and spatial trends (segmented regression and geographic mapping).

Findings: D2 identified nearly twice as many asymptomatic cases as D1 (14.74% vs. 8.29%, difference +6.45%, p<0.001), reclassifying 67,022 (6.5%). Risk factor associations were attenuated under D2: odds ratios for 41/46 subgroups shifted toward 1.0, reducing discriminative power. Temporal trends showed a national peak in early 2022 then decline, with marked provincial heterogeneity. Geographic disparities were more pronounced under D1, revealing a strong south-to-north gradient.

Interpretation Asymptomatic TB definition choice affects epidemiological estimates, risk factor identification, and geographic patterns. The stricter definition (D1) better captures screening-relevant populations and should be considered for standardizing surveillance and guiding active case-finding in high-burden settings.

title: Beyond Tick Box Compliance: Worker Rights, Legal Accountability and Institutional Reform in UK Healthcare

detail.title: Beyond Tick Box Compliance: Worker Rights, Legal Accountability and Institutional Reform in UK Healthcare
detail.abstract: This paper examines legal compliance in UK healthcare institutions and argues that worker protection cannot be reduced to policies, dashboards, audit trails and procedural reporting. Although the United Kingdom has a mature legal framework covering employment rights, health and safety, equality, harassment and whistleblowing, recent evidence from NHS workforce data, Care Quality Commission materials, Freedom to Speak Up reporting and social care workforce analysis shows a persistent gap between formal compliance and lived protection. The paper adopts a structured legal and health policy review, drawing on statute, regulatory guidance, public inquiry findings, NHS workforce evidence and selected academic literature. It develops a Substantive Compliance Framework to explain how healthcare organisations can move from documentation to practical legal accountability. The framework focuses on five connected domains: secure and lawful employment, safe systems of work, equality and dignity, speaking up and whistleblowing, and board level accountability. The analysis shows that tick box compliance is not a harmless administrative habit. It can normalise unsafe staffing, weak responses to violence and stress, superficial equality monitoring, insecure care work and fear of raising concerns. The paper recommends outcome based board reporting, stronger Care Quality Commission assessment of workforce rights, targeted enforcement in domiciliary care, proactive prevention of sexual harassment, investment in rights literacy, better use of workforce data and closer integration between worker wellbeing and patient safety governance. It concludes that substantive compliance is not separate from healthcare quality. In UK healthcare, protecting workers is a condition of safe, lawful and trustworthy care.

title: Tribal Agriculture in Arizona An Economic Contribution Analysis
affiliations: University of Arizona, , University of Arizona, University of Arizona and University of Arizona

detail.title: Tribal Agriculture in Arizona An Economic Contribution Analysis
detail.abstract:
Arizona's twenty-two federally recognized tribes have practiced agriculture for thousands of years, developing sophisticated systems based on ecological knowledge, water management, and crop diversity. These systems are key to tribal economies, cultural identity, and food sovereignty. However, despite its importance, the state-wide economic role of tribal agriculture has been scarcely studied.


This report provides a systematic profile of tribal agriculture using the best publicly available data and methods. We conduct a comprehensive benchmark of tribal agriculture’s economic contribution in Arizona, the first to our knowledge. The main goal of this report is to serve as a foundation for future research, improved understanding, and more refined analyses over time. The report does not quantify other critical values of tribal agricultural production such as cultural values, nutritional and public health benefits, food sovereignty, and environmental values. Nonetheless, this study provides a needed baseline assessment of existing tribal agricultural activity in Arizona.

title: The Impact of the Energy Transition on Local Mortality
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology - School of Economics, University of Kentucky and

detail.title: The Impact of the Energy Transition on Local Mortality
detail.abstract: The health consequences of sectoral transitions are theoretically ambiguous. Reductions in industrial activity and associated pollution may improve health, while local economic deterioration may worsen it. This paper examines these competing forces in the context of coal’s decline. Linking restricted-access mortality data with detailed records of coal-fired power plant and mine activity from 2004 to 2019, we find that power-sector contractions reduce pollution-related mortality among older adults, while coal mining contractions increase mortality and overdose deaths among working-age adults. These results indicate that the health consequences of coal’s decline depend not only on pollution reductions, but also the uneven economic disruptions experienced by coal-dependent communities.

title: Diversification Under Stress: Empirical Evidence of Correlation Breakdown Across Sectors and International Markets
affiliations: ETH Zürich

detail.title: Diversification Under Stress: Empirical Evidence of Correlation Breakdown Across Sectors and International Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether portfolio diversification across U.S. sectors and international equity markets retains its risk-reducing properties under stress. Using daily return data from 1999 to 2025 spanning ten sector ETFs and eight international equity indices, we document a systematic correlation breakdown: mean pairwise correlations rise significantly during crisis episodes, precisely when diversification would be most valuable. Across nine crisis periods and 59 systematically identified stress events, correlations increase in 71.2 % of all cases, with a mean ∆ρ = 0.094 that is statistically highly significant (p < 0.0001). We show that the nature of a shock matters more than its magnitude: idiosyncratic events leave correlations intact, while systemic shocks produce strong co-movement across all sectors simultaneously. Sector and international diversification fail together in systemic crises but diverge in idiosyncratic ones, a distinction that, to our knowledge, has not been systematically documented across this breadth of episodes. We introduce the Trachsler Resilience Score, a formal criterion for selecting sectors that are robust to correlation breakdown under stress, and validate it out-of-sample: the Resilience Portfolio reduces maximum drawdown in 83 % of independent stress events (p = 0.003). Our findings suggest that naive diversification offers substantially less protection than classical portfolio theory implies, and that crisis-conditional correlation structure should be an explicit input to portfolio construction.

title: Do Unconditional Cash Transfers Reduce Homelessness? A Conceptual Self-Replication
affiliations: , UBC Faculty of Medicine and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Department of Psychology

detail.title: Do Unconditional Cash Transfers Reduce Homelessness? A Conceptual Self-Replication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The current experiment received approval from UBC Behavioural Research Ethics Board (H21-02584).
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by Foundations for Social Change, Mitacs, and UBC Stone Centre on Wealth and Income Inequality.

detail.abstract: The lack of financial resources has emerged as a leading cause of homelessness in North America. In response, a growing body of literature has shown the promise of unconditional cash transfers as a tool to address homelessness. The current study is a conceptual self-replication to examine the impact of unconditional cash transfers on individuals experiencing homelessness. In this pre-registered randomized controlled trial, we distributed an unconditional cash transfer of CAD$8,500 to each of 98 individuals experiencing homelessness, with another 112 as controls in Vancouver, BC. Pre-registered analyses showed that over the first three months cash participants spent more days in stable housing, retained more savings, spent more overall and on temptation goods, with no change in days in literal homelessness, shelter use costs, and rent spending. Exploratory analyses showed that over one year cash participants spent 54 fewer days homeless, retained a higher value of savings ($2,583) and belongings ($1,968), and spent more ($5,616). Those with regular employment worked eight more hours per week and had higher hourly pay ($5), while those with casual employment worked six fewer hours per week. Among social assistance recipients, cash participants received smaller payments ($98) than control participants. Cash participants also experienced greater autonomy, competence, food security, and fluid intelligence, and less psychological distress and fewer education hours. The current study advances the theoretical understanding of cash transfers providing the financial freedom to secure housing, and actionable policy insights on the design of targeted cash transfers to better address the financial drivers of homelessness.

title: Sticky Expectations, Active Fiscal Transfers, and the Post-Pandemic Inflation
affiliations: UCLA

detail.title: Sticky Expectations, Active Fiscal Transfers, and the Post-Pandemic Inflation
detail.abstract: During the inflationary surge of 2021-2023, inflation expectations were slow to rise-but when they did, expected real interest rates fell as nominal rate expectations remained roughly constant. I estimate a medium-scale sticky-expectations heterogeneous agent New Keynesian (HANK) model and study the effect of fiscal transfers under a policy configuration that matches this expectations pattern. In particular, I simulate the deficit-financed transfers disbursed by the CARES Act of 2020 and the Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA) and the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) of 2021 in a scenario wherein the central bank does not systematically respond to inflation with higher interest rates and the government does not commit to retire past deficits with future taxation. The simulated payments boost real annual GDP relative to trend by an average of 0.6% per quarter over 2020Q1-2023Q4 with an overall transfer multiplier of 2.0 and reduces unemployment by an average of 1.5 percentage points in each quarter. However, they also induce a 4.2% surge in the price level over the same period, with a peak annual inflation rate in 2022 of 2.8% above trend (slightly less than half of the post-pandemic peak observed in the data). This contrasts with the highly muted response of unemployment and inflation to similar fiscal shocks in an environment wherein all agents believe the central bank will raise interest rates in response to inflation. Unlike the first setting, this latter environment yields an expectations pattern that differs strongly from the post-2020 expectations data.

title: When Oil Falters, Gas and Coal Rise: A Volatility-Spillover Tale for Energy Stocks
affiliations: , Eastern Mediterranean University - Department of Banking and Finance and Eastern Mediterranean University

detail.title: When Oil Falters, Gas and Coal Rise: A Volatility-Spillover Tale for Energy Stocks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This study investigates volatility spillovers, network connectedness, and hedging strategies among major fossil fuels and energy stock indices in the five highest fossil fuels-consuming countries from 2008 to 2024. Using TVP-VAR and DCC-GARCH models, we examine how geopolitical and economic shocks influence market interactions. Results show that volatility connectedness increases during turbulent periods, peaking during the COVID-19 pandemic. Brent crude oil incurs the highest hedging cost and delivers the strongest hedging effectiveness in the full sample. However, its effectiveness deteriorates during oil-specific supply shocks. Natural gas and coal display low correlations with energy stock indices, making them the most cost-effective hedges. Regime-based hedging effectiveness analysis reveals that natural gas is countercyclical, strengthening precisely when oil-based hedges weaken. Coal hedging is highly regime-dependent, with its viability contingent on a country's energy structure and the source of market stress. The findings highlight the need for adaptive, regime-sensitive hedging strategies.

title: The Community Navigator programme for people with treatment resistant depression in community mental health teams in England: randomised controlled trial

detail.abstract:
Background:  Outcomes are poor for many people with treatment resistant depression (TRD). Loneliness is independently associated with poorer recovery from depression and constitutes a novel TRD treatment target. A previous feasibility trial of a social intervention to target depression and loneliness in this group, the Community Navigator programme, showed the intervention was feasible and acceptable.

Methods: We completed an individual randomised controlled trial of the co-developed Community Navigator programme plus usual Community Mental Health Team (CMHT) care, compared to usual CMHT care plus an information booklet about local social groups. The primary outcome was change in depression symptoms (PHQ-9 scale) at 8-months (end-of-treatment).The Community Navigator programme offered up to 10 individual meetings with a Community Navigator and up to four group sessions. Community Navigators who had expertise in supporting social participation delivered the manualised programme. They mapped participants’ social worlds and supported them to set and achieve desired social connections goals.

Findings: We recruited 313 participants and completed follow-ups with 271 for the primary outcome. Of 158 intervention group participants, 76% were treated per protocol. At the end-of-treatment (8-months), PHQ-9 depression score in the intervention group was 0.91 units lower than in the usual care group but this was not significant (95% CI: -0.53 to 2.36, P=0.204). A significant result was only found for one of nine secondary outcomes at end-of-treatment (depression substantial improvement), and for no outcomes at 14-month follow-up. The programme was not cost-effective.

Interpretation: The Community Navigator programme as delivered cannot be recommended for use in practice for people with TRD. Further research is needed to develop effective treatments for TRD and programmes to alleviate loneliness in mental health populations generally.

title: Women's Age at Marriage and Clean Cooking Fuel Adoption in India
affiliations: , Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad and Zayed University

detail.title: Women's Age at Marriage and Clean Cooking Fuel Adoption in India
detail.abstract: A substantial share of households in developing countries continues to rely on traditional biomass fuels for cooking despite the associated adverse consequences for public health, environmental quality, and household welfare. Using nationally representative data from India, we examine the causal impact of women's age at marriage on uptake of clean cooking fuel. To address endogeneity in marriage timing, we employ an instrumental-variable strategy that uses women's age at menarche as an instrument for age at marriage. Our results indicate that a one-year delay in women's age at marriage increases the probability of clean cooking fuel adoption by approximately 2.1 percentage points. Given India's scale, the implied aggregate effects are economically meaningful and suggest that improvements in women's life-course outcomes can contribute to broader energy transitions. Further, we find that delaying marriages improves women's educational attainment, literacy, and intrahousehold decision-making power, which in turn increase the likelihood of clean fuel use. Our findings underscore the need for policies that seek to delay women's age at marriage along with interventions that provide financial support to families for girls' education. The results highlight the complementarity between gender empowerment policies and clean energy transitions in developing economies.

title: Trust Experience Glitches: AI Agents, Delegated Autonomy, and the Breakdown of Legal Assumptions
affiliations: New York University Shanghai

detail.title: Trust Experience Glitches: AI Agents, Delegated Autonomy, and the Breakdown of Legal Assumptions
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is shifting from a technology of output generation to a technology of delegated action. Beyond answering queries in a chat window, contemporary AI agents can call APIs, manage credentials, write and deploy code, move money, negotiate with other agents, and act across digital environments autonomously with limited human supervision. This shift unsettles legal frameworks that assume clear delegation, identifiable actors, traceable causation, revocable authority, and enforceable defendants. This paper introduces the concept of the trust experience glitch: a discrete rupture in a stakeholder's reasonable trust expectations at the moment an autonomous AI system acts. A trust experience glitch is not merely a bug, hallucination, or AI incident, but rather a relational failure that exposes a mismatch between the trust signals emitted by a system or platform and the behavior stakeholders actually experience. Drawing on documented agentic AI failures, this paper develops a six-part taxonomy of trust experience glitches: (1) agency assertion, (2) epistemic camouflage, (3) delegation ambiguity, (4) opacity at scale, (5) cascading autonomy, and (6) revocation failure. It then maps these failure modes onto legal assumptions under strain: authority, veracity, causation, consent, and enforceability. This paper argues that agentic AI does not simply create new liability risks, but reveals a deeper mismatch between ex-post legal remedies and systems whose harmful actions may be distributed, opaque, emergent, or difficult to stop. The appropriate governance response must therefore move upstream, from after-the-fact attribution to protocol-level constraints. It concludes by pointing to a set of protocol primitives as the "traffic lights" of the agentic web.

title: Strong Wills, Strong Outcomes? Bank Resolvability and Credit Supply
affiliations: and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: Strong Wills, Strong Outcomes? Bank Resolvability and Credit Supply
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of resolvability as a new regulatory constraint for restricting bank behaviour. Using a regression-discontinuity design, we exploit the 2019 regulatory shock that made banks with assets below the $250 billion asset threshold exempt to “living will” requirements. We find that affected banks experience an increase in their profitability and their shareholder value. They also lend more and at more favourable terms. Credit granting is boosted especially in less resolvable loans with no covenant restrictions and in countries with poor creditor rights. Our findings suggest that by enforcing crisis plans, “living wills” may contract credit supply.

title: Beyond Bounties: Implicit Financial Motives in Non-Monetary Whistleblowing
affiliations: Xiamen National Accounting Institute, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU)

detail.title: Beyond Bounties: Implicit Financial Motives in Non-Monetary Whistleblowing
detail.abstract: Why do employees blow the whistle and risk employer retaliation in the absence of explicit monetary rewards? We hypothesize that whistleblowing provides implicit financial benefits: by reducing workplace accident risk, reporting safety hazards protects employees' income stability and future earnings. To test this hypothesis, we exploit variation in household wealth arising from local housing price fluctuations among employees working at different facilities of the same parent firm, which captures differences in employees' demand for income stability. We find that a onestandard-deviation decline in local housing prices increases whistleblowing complaints by 6% and the probability of detecting a violation by 5%. In addition, the probability of a workplace injury decreases by 5%. These effects are stronger in areas with high blue-collar homeownership, when unemployment insurance reduces the economic cost of job loss (from employer retaliation), and at facilities with a prior record of safety violations, where safety risks and enforcement are more salient. In contrast, the effects are weaker when employees have greater non-housing wealth. Our findings indicate that workplace safety considerations act as implicit financial incentives that encourage whistleblowing. More broadly, we extend the literature on compensating wage differentials by showing that workers engage in non-wage, self-protective actions when formal compensation for job risk is incomplete.

title: Fairness Trade-offs in Expert Evaluation: Information, Judgment, and Procedural Design
affiliations: University of Southern Denmark and University of Vermont - Department of Economics

detail.title: Fairness Trade-offs in Expert Evaluation: Information, Judgment, and Procedural Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Evaluation systems often seek to reduce bias, prevent manipulation, preserve relevant information, maintain comparability, and treat candidates equally, but these fairness goals can conflict. This paper develops a framework for understanding such trade-offs in expert evaluation---including peer review, grant panels, academic hiring, and artistic competitions---where quality is multidimensional and legitimate disagreement among evaluators is possible. We treat the choice among evaluation procedures as a problem of constitutional design: rules must be selected before the specific candidates, evaluators, and circumstances that will test them are known. Classical music competitions are our primary analytical setting because their rules, scores, and controversies make these trade-offs unusually visible, but the framework applies to other settings in which expert judgments are aggregated under incomplete information. The framework highlights two core tensions: information control and outlier rules. First, when information is both quality-relevant and identity-revealing, procedures that suppress bias-relevant cues may also remove information with genuine evaluative content. Second, because sincere minority judgment and strategic manipulation can generate similar observed score patterns, score-based exclusion rules may reduce manipulation while limiting legitimate dissent. Two further trade-offs concerning transparency and standardization are developed as illustrations. The analysis shows that no procedure can eliminate all vulnerabilities at once, and well-intentioned reforms may weaken the very values they aim to protect.

title: Climate Change and Sustainability:a Multicriteria Perspective
affiliations: University of Milan, Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM)) and University of Pisa

detail.title: Climate Change and Sustainability:a Multicriteria Perspective
detail.abstract: We introduce sustainability considerations in an integrated assessment model of climate change byanalyzing the implications of the social welfare function. The traditional social welfare function based ondiscounted utilitarianism cannot account for intertemporal equity thus different alternatives have beenproposed, such as the green golden rule and the Chinchilnisky criterion. The latter consists of a weightedaverage between discounted utilitarianism and the green golden rule, giving rise to a multicriteria formulationof the climate mitigation problem in which the scalarization factor is represented by the relativeweight between the two criteria measured by the degree of sustainability concern. We assess how theoptimal mitigation policy changes in alternative scenarios under different values of this parameter, characterizingthe extent to which sustainability considerations affect the intensity of environmental policiesalong with their implications on the efficient frontier. We show that climate mitigation is highly sensitiveto the degree of sustainability concern, and the more we care for long run sustainability the stricter thepolicy measures and the earlier the optimal timing of carbon neutrality.

title: Between Toolkit and Theory: A Critical Review of Social Metabolism
affiliations: Universidad Pablo de Olavide, University of Granada - Department of Economic Theory and Economic History and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Between Toolkit and Theory: A Critical Review of Social Metabolism
detail.abstract: Social Metabolism (SM) has generated a growing body of literature. From its inception, SM carried a dual ambition: to develop biophysical accounting tools rather than solely in monetary units, and to build a theory of socio-ecological change. Yet methodological ambition has largely overshadowed the theoretical one, and the research communities that have developed around SM remain fragmented. No systematic theoretical characterization of these schools of thought currently exists. This paper proposes such a characterization. Building on a comprehensive bibliometric corpus of over 4,700 publications, we conduct a critical qualitative review that identifies four main schools of SM: the Vienna School (VS/MEFA), the MuSIASEM school, the Metabolic Rift school (MR), and the Social Agrarian Metabolism school (SAM). We compare them across six analytical dimensions: terminology and definitions, epistemological scope, operational tools, stock/flow vs. fund/flow approaches, main applications, and the integration of social variables. We examine not only how each school measures biophysical flows, but how it conceptualizes the relationship between society and nature and how far it has developed SM as a genuine socio-ecological theory. We conclude by identifying key challenges, including the need to recover the original theoretical ambition of SM as a comprehensive framework for understanding socio-ecological change

title: Patent Litigation Finance and the Venture Capital Myth

detail.title: Patent Litigation Finance and the Venture Capital Myth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Managing Director—IP Investments & General Counsel at Parabellum Capital, a commercial litigation finance firm. The article addresses claims about the patent litigation finance industry, in which Parabellum Capital is a market participant. The views expressed are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect those of Parabellum Capital.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This Article is a doctrinal and empirical analysis of public market data and published legal scholarship. It does not involve human subjects research.

detail.abstract:
A recent Sedona Conference Journal article contends that patent litigation funders employ a "venture capital model," financing high volumes of low-merit cases on the theory that occasional outsized winners will offset losses of 50 to 70 percent. The authors use that descriptive claim about how the asset class operates to motivate disclosure and fee-shifting reforms.

This Article shows that the VC model is not a strategy any rational patent litigation funder would pursue, and the available evidence indicates that none in fact does. The analysis proceeds along three lines.

The evidentiary basis for the VC model claim is one enforcement campaign and two individual cases. None produced the collectible outlier recovery the theory requires. The strategy also fails as a matter of fund mathematics. A portfolio carrying 50 to 70 percent losses requires winners large enough to cover the lost capital and clear the return hurdles that allow a manager to raise a successor fund. Patent damages are bounded by statute and doctrine, compressed on appeal, and realized over decade-long timelines. Recent empirical work shows damages awards above $500 million have a 0 percent survival rate on appeal. The patent system does not produce the collectible tail outcomes the VC model requires.

The publicly reported returns of Burford Capital and Omni Bridgeway, the two largest publicly traded funders, show loss rates of 15 and 22 percent of deployed capital and moderate, distributed winners rather than rare lottery payoffs. That is the opposite of a VC-style return profile.

Patent litigation finance is viable because competent practitioners do the opposite of what the VC model describes. The asset class rewards selectivity, not variance. Reform proposals grounded in an inaccurate description of the market produce unsound policy.

title: Managing the Institutional Tradeoffs Between Water Market Efficiency and Reservoir Sustainability
affiliations: Regis University, Siena College and New Mexico State University

detail.title: Managing the Institutional Tradeoffs Between Water Market Efficiency and Reservoir Sustainability
detail.abstract: Climate change and prolonged drought are intensifying pressure on water allocation institutions in arid river basins worldwide. In the Lower Colorado River Basin, declining inflows and falling reservoir storage have renewed debate over how alternative allocation systems affect both economic performance and long-term hydrologic sustainability. While previous studies have examined water markets and economic efficiency, there remains a critical gap in understanding how institutional flexibility influences the tradeoff between consumptive water use and reservoir storage under climate drought. To address this gap, we use a dynamic, hydro-economic optimization model, calibrated to observed hydrologic and economic data between 2000 and 2021, to provide the first evidence of how water allocation institutions influence economic efficiency, water use, shadow prices, and reservoir storage. Three allocation institutions are evaluated: interstate markets, intrastate markets, and proportional sharing within state economic sectors. Results show that institutional flexibility increases economic efficiency but also increases pressure on reservoir storage. Interstate trading, the most flexible institution, generates the highest economic benefits and lowest marginal scarcity values, indicating more efficient reallocation of water to higher-valued uses. However, these gains are accompanied by lower average Lake Mead storage due to higher basin-wide consumptive use. In contrast, proportional sectoral sharing yields the lowest economic returns but conserves higher storage. Differences among institutions become more pronounced as drought severity increases.

title: Carving spaces for alternatives in a capitalist world? Political economy in pluriversal transformations
affiliations: University of Helsinki

detail.title: Carving spaces for alternatives in a capitalist world? Political economy in pluriversal transformations
detail.abstract: Strategies for post-growth transformations are increasingly turning toward "pluriversal" transformations: reducing social metabolism through locally embedded, small-scale initiatives grounded in alternative ontologies and epistemologies. This turn has reopened generative questions about what counts as transformation and whose knowledge legitimately organizes it. Yet recent critiques argue that pluriversal scholarship leaves the political-economic conditions in which such transformations are embedded largely unexamined. This paper asks how does the political-economic conditions shape the possibilities for pluriversal transformations? Drawing on 34 semi-structured interviews with government officials, municipal representatives, academics, NGOs, and indigenous community members in Ecuador - a country whose 2008 Constitution enshrined Buen Vivir, Rights of Nature, and a social and solidarity economy - the paper identifies how the different actors across grassroots and state saw transformations being shaped, enabled, and foreclosed. The findings reveal three interlocking tensions: an ontological conflict over what counts as economic value, structural fiscal and debt dependencies that locked the state into extractivism, and global political-economic pressures that wore down community alternatives even as they sustained non-monetary provisioning, food sovereignty, and resistance to mining. The paper argues that political economy is constitutive, not incidental, to pluriversal transformations, and that carving durable space for pluriversal alternatives requires a different political economy of the state - one capable of recognizing non-monetary value and shielding territorial alternatives from capital's expansionary logic. Whether this is possible within a global capitalist economy remains an open question, but one the field can no longer defer.

title: Designing results-based collective PES in Ecuadorian mangroves: an expert- and stakeholder-based analysis
affiliations: Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Designing results-based collective PES in Ecuadorian mangroves: an expert- and stakeholder-based analysis
detail.abstract: Mangrove ecosystems are vital common-pool resources which are under threat. Collective payments for ecosystem services (cPES) are suitable schemes for ensuring their conservation. However, there is an important knowledge gap on how the type of payment—compensatory or incentivizing, practice- or results-based—determines resource users’ willingness to accept (WTA) for participation in these voluntary schemes, especially in the context of mangroves. Drawing on a case study of Ecuadorian mangroves where an unsuccessful cPES scheme has been implemented, the present study relies on a best-worst discrete choice experiment (BWDCE) and an indirect valuation approach using experts’ and resource users’ choice information. Results reveal a significant discrepancy between expert predictions and user preferences: while experts favor stringent results-based targets and compensatory collective payments, resource users strongly prefer incentives, especially collective ones. Furthermore, resource users accept moderate ecological targets but reject highly stringent requirements and increases in the minimum eligible area. Transitioning toward more enabling cPES designs—characterized by moderate conditionality and collective incentives—can bridge the gap between technical conservation goals and local management logic, ultimately strengthening mangrove governance and coastal resilience.

title: Thematic Evolution and Collaboration Networks in Character Education: A Bibliometric Perspective
