A Jurisprudential Look at when Profit comes before Justice
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces NeoJuris Theory, a jurisprudential framework examining how legitimacy operates within increasingly complex institutional, procedural, and technological systems. The framework  focuses on three central conditions of institutional legitimacy: legibility, verifiability, and accountability alignment. As modern legal and administrative systems become more dependent upon informational abstraction, automated decision-making, procedural layering, and distributed authority, ordinary participants increasingly struggle to understand how decisions are reached, where responsibility resides, and who ultimately absorbs institutional risk when systems fail.

Rather than arguing that modern institutions are inherently illegitimate, NeoJuris Theory examines how procedural distance and informational opacity can weaken public trust even where formal compliance with legal rules remains intact. The paper explores these dynamics across litigation environments, technological systems, arbitration structures, digital platforms, and broader institutional frameworks where complexity itself may function as a form of structural insulation. 

The paper further develops the concept of “absorbed risk,” examining how contemporary systems may externalize operational burdens downward while distributing procedural insulation upward. Ultimately, the framework argues that legitimacy depends not only upon the existence of procedural rules, but upon whether accountability remains proportionate to institutional power and whether ordinary individuals can meaningfully understand the systems exercising authority over them.

title: Perceptions of Chemical and Microbial Irrigation Water Quality Among Agricultural Workers in Mbeya, Tanzania
affiliations: University of Maryland School of Public Health, University of Maryland School of Public Health, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Maryland School of Public Health, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Sokoine University of Agriculture, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Maryland School of Public Health

detail.title: Perceptions of Chemical and Microbial Irrigation Water Quality Among Agricultural Workers in Mbeya, Tanzania
detail.abstract: Agricultural workers’ perceptions of irrigation water quality influence their water management practices, impacting food safety and public health. However, there are no known data on the perceptions of agricultural workers in Mbeya, Tanzania, regarding the chemical and microbial quality of irrigation water, as well as the associated health risks. To address this data gap, we conducted a cross-sectional survey from September to October 2024 among agricultural workers (n=171) in Mbeya, Tanzania. Descriptive statistics and logistic regression were performed using SAS and R. Awareness of the importance of irrigation water quality was high among agricultural workers, as 78% of agricultural workers agreed that poor water quality can negatively impact agricultural output, and 62% acknowledged poor irrigation water quality as a contributing factor to health problems in their communities. Men were more likely to report being knowledgeable about chemical contaminants (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 3.42, 95% CI: 1.68–6.96, p = <0.001) and microbial contaminants (aOR = 2.87, 95% CI: 1.41–5.83, p = 0.004) compared to women. The importance of regular water quality testing also differed by gender. Men were more likely than women to report that they understood the importance of water testing (aOR = 2.52, 95% CI: 1.26–5.04, p = 0.009). Our findings are the first of their kind from Mbeya, Tanzania, revealing significant gaps in agricultural workers’ understanding of chemical and microbiological contaminants in irrigation water and highlighting the need for targeted education and capacity-building initiatives to improve irrigation water quality management practices in this area.

title: Science on the Move: How Experiential Pedagogy Shapes Human Capital
affiliations: , New York University (NYU) - New York University, Abu Dhabi,  and Northeastern University (USA)

detail.title: Science on the Move: How Experiential Pedagogy Shapes Human Capital

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite near-universal school enrollment across many developing economies, the provision of quality education that cultivates lifelong learning and the capacity to apply knowledge in novel circumstances remains elusive. We conduct a cluster-randomized controlled trial in 132 public schools in Uttar Pradesh, India, to evaluate a guided, discovery-based science pedagogy at two intensity levels: a high-intensity Mobile Science Lab (MSL) and a lower-intensity Lab on Bike (LoB). MSL improves motivational beliefs and self-confidence by 0.15-0.18 standard deviations, reduces perceived barriers to education by 0.23 standard deviations, raises engagement by 0.17-0.22 standard deviations, and increases standardized test scores by 0.22-0.34 standard deviations across all subjects. LoB produces limited average effects, with gains concentrated among students completing all sessions. These findings demonstrate that pedagogical design and delivery intensity are critical determinants of multidimensional human capital formation, and that discovery-based pedagogy can shift motivational beliefs, engagement, and achievement in low-capacity public school systems.

title: A Practical Guide to Instrumental Variables Methods with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
affiliations: Brandeis University - Department of Economics,  and Independent

detail.title: A Practical Guide to Instrumental Variables Methods with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Instrumental variables (IV) methods are central to applied microeconomics. While classical approaches assume linear models with constant effects, recent literature has shifted toward the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework to accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects. This paper provides a practical guide to aligning empirical practice with recent theory. We first examine how different specifications with covariates lead to distinct weighted averages of covariate-specific LATEs. We then discuss how parametric misspecification can undermine the causal interpretation of these estimands and suggest flexible specifications as essential robustness checks. Finally, we review formal tests for LATE assumptions and methods robust to monotonicity violations. We provide a guide to software implementations to help researchers apply the methods in practice.

title: Intergenerational Transmission of Victimization
affiliations: , University of Copenhagen, University of Oxford - Department of Economics, University of Copenhagen and University of Warwick

detail.title: Intergenerational Transmission of Victimization

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using four decades of Danish administrative data, we estimate the intergenerational transmission of violent crime victimization. Sons are twice as likely, and daughters three times as likely, to be victimized if a parent was victimized, with stronger associations if the mother was the victim. Controlling for cohort, municipality, socioeconomic factors, parental cohabitation, and parental offending explains about 60% of this correlation. The link is weaker in higher-income families; it persists for sons, but is driven to zero for daughters. Further, children of victimized parents experience lower absolute income mobility, comparable to the Black-White difference for men in the United States.

title: Hypocrisy in a Simple Social Interaction Model
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney (UTS), European University at St. Petersburg (EUSP) and University of the Balearic Islands

detail.title: Hypocrisy in a Simple Social Interaction Model

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a model of social interaction in which agents hold private beliefs but communicate public statements. We distinguish between two networks: an audience network shaping statements through social pressure, and an influence network governing belief updating. This separation drives a wedge between public statements and underlying beliefs, so that agents may persistently communicate opinions they do not hold. We provide necessary and sufficient network conditions for the emergence of such hypocrisy. The model generates rich patterns of opinion propagation, including the amplification of messages that agents themselves do not believe, and sheds light on phenomena such as propaganda diffusion, the spiral of silence, and political correctness.

title: La Bohème? Labour Market Outcomes among Artists in Europe and the Effects of Cultural Policy
affiliations: and

detail.title: La Bohème? Labour Market Outcomes among Artists in Europe and the Effects of Cultural Policy

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper documents the labour market position of artists across Europe and examines how public cultural spending is related to artists' outcomes. Using EU-LFS micro-data for 2009--2023, we compare artists to non-artists using harmonised measures of wage rank, employment, and non-standard work. Using within-country variation and controlling for demographic factors, artists rank substantially lower in the wage distribution: in the pooled sample, the estimated penalty is about 0.46 wage deciles relative to other salaried workers and about 0.28 deciles relative to other professionals. These earnings gaps coexist with higher exposure to non-standard employment, including part-time work, temporary contracts, and multiple job holding, with patterns that persist over the life cycle and appear in most countries. We then link individual outcomes to a country-year panel of real per capita public expenditure on cultural services. Higher cultural spending is associated with modest improvements in aggregate employment and a lower incidence of part-time work, but these associations do not systematically differ for artists or arts graduates. The only consistent differential correlation is an increase in multiple job holding among arts graduates in higher-spending environments. Thus, changes in aggregate cultural spending are not sufficient on their own to narrow wage or job-quality gaps for artists, motivating a rethinking of cultural policy instruments toward mechanisms that more directly address labour market risks faced by cultural workers.

title: Dishonesty in Complex Environments: Deliberate Lies, Shortcuts, or Accidental Mistakes?
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance and Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance

detail.title: Dishonesty in Complex Environments: Deliberate Lies, Shortcuts, or Accidental Mistakes?

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Compliance with complex regulatory requirements can be challenging. We study why and how complexity affects non-compliance in terms of incorrect reporting. Our novel experimental design isolates two distinct complexity effects: an increase in honest mistakes and a substantial shift toward self-serving dishonesty. We identify two mechanisms for this dishonesty shift. First, individuals with social image concerns systematically take advantage of plausible deniability. Second, we document an unexplored form of dishonesty: besides conscious lies, individuals use fraudulent shortcuts in response to complex cheating opportunities.

title: Economic Relations between Bangladesh and Spain: An Empirical Analysis of Trade, Demographics, and Sectoral Growth (2000-2025)

detail.title: Economic Relations between Bangladesh and Spain: An Empirical Analysis of Trade, Demographics, and Sectoral Growth (2000-2025)
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the bilateral economic corridor between Bangladesh and Spain (2000-2025). Using an augmented gravity model with HAC standard errors, results reveal that Bangladesh's export volume is highly elastic with respect to domestic GDP growth (β = 2.20) and decoupled from Spanish business cycles. Structural break analysis shows that post-2013 compliance reforms increased buyer trust, although growth elasticity is maturing. Building on evidence from sustainable finance, the paper argues that after Bangladesh's LDC graduation in 2029, high-transparency ESG lending will be essential to meet EU requirements. The strategic recommendations, therefore, emphasize industrial upgrading and export diversification to sustain this important economic partnership.

title: Quantifying Pastoral Economic Resilience Using CAL Metric Analysis of Climate Adaptation in Kenya
affiliations: Egerton University, Egerton University and Egerton University

detail.title: Quantifying Pastoral Economic Resilience Using CAL Metric Analysis of Climate Adaptation in Kenya
detail.abstract: Droughts and erratic rainfall are the primary climate challenges affecting pastoral livelihoods across Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands. This challenge is compounded by a lack of rigorous quantitative evidence on households' long-term adaptive capacity. This study uses Cumulative Adaptation Level (CAL) metric to measure economic resilience by integrating livestock asset retention, adaptation strategy breadth, coping ease, and food security into composite indices. The study draws on a household survey of 490 pastoral households in Kajiado County, Kenya, focusing on the adoption of soil bunding (53.3%) as the focal nature-based intervention. The mean CAL metric (0.605, SD = 0.111) reveals substantial heterogeneity in resilience, which is invisible to single-indicator proxies. Raw comparisons indicate adverse selection, as adopters face higher drought exposure, lower incomes, and greater food insecurity than non-adopters, producing a spurious negative CAL gap of -0.002. Propensity-score matching corrects this bias, yielding an ATT of +0.007, with adopters showing broader adaptation portfolios and fewer months of food insecurity. The economic case for scaling is established through revealed preference. Adopters contribute 92.2 man-days of labour per household, valued at KES[1] 46, 46,094, exceeding estimated construction costs by 2-4 times. Heterogeneity analysis identifies low TLUb and female-headed households as the highest-return adoption targets. The study contributes a replicable CAL framework for measuring dryland resilience and demonstrates that correcting for adverse selection is essential for a credible evaluation of nature-based adaptation investments.    [1] KES refers to Kenyan Shilling (Official Kenyan Currency) Exchange rate was 1$US =129.00 at the time of the survey

title: Digital Payments and Economic Performance: Evidence from Italy

detail.title: Digital Payments and Economic Performance: Evidence from Italy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy: Markets, Infrastructures, Payment Systems No. 80
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between the use of digital payments and economic performance across Italian provinces from 2012 to 2023. Using a novel dataset drawn from the statistical sources of Banca d’Italia, Istat and Cerved, we construct granular indicators of digital payment usage, including card transactions, account‑to‑account (A2A) transfers and e‑commerce activity. By employing a dynamic panel framework that is estimated using System‑GMM, we find a robust positive association between digital payment intensity and nominal GDP per capita. Provinces with greater per‑capita card usage and A2A transfers exhibit a stronger economic performance, a pattern corroborated by broader measures of digital intensity, such as online‑initiated payments. While our empirical strategy addresses several endogeneity concerns, the results are not strictly causal. They suggest that greater uptake of digital payments is associated with a stronger economic performance and may reflect broader technological and economic modernization.

title: Re-estimated FR-BDF: New Features and an Assessment of Monetary Policy Tightening in France
affiliations: Banque de France, Banque de France, Banque de France, Banque de France, Banque de France,  and Banque de France

detail.title: Re-estimated FR-BDF: New Features and an Assessment of Monetary Policy Tightening in France

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. No. 1044
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper presents the updated and re-estimated version of the Banque de France's semi-structural FR-BDF model, the institution's core framework for quarterly projections and policy scenario analysis. The update reflects major statistical and structural shifts, including INSEE's transition to a 2020 base year and the volatility during the COVID-19 period. The re-estimated model features a lower capital share, a weaker underlying productivity trend, a steeper price Phillips curve along with a flatter wage Phillips curve, while adding a credit block and an enhanced consumption equation that captures short-run income effects. The updated FR-BDF delivers stronger and faster real effects of monetary policy-with larger GDP and unemployment responses due to amplified transmission through long-term rates and the exchange rate-while nominal responses are more muted. Using the updated model, the recent monetary tightening is assessed to lower VA inflation by-0.6 pp and reduce GDP growth by 1 pp (at trough) under backward-looking expectations, whereas under forward-looking expectations the responses are more front-loaded and nearly three times larger. Under the more realistic hybrid expectations mode, VA inflation falls by about 1.2 percentage points and GDP growth by roughly 2 percentage points at the trough. These magnitudes remain broadly consistent with benchmark assessments reported in the literature.

title: Magnaporthiopsis paspali  associated with root disease of seashore paspalum in Hainan, China

detail.title: Magnaporthiopsis paspali  associated with root disease of seashore paspalum in Hainan, China
detail.abstract: Seashore paspalum (Paspalum vaginatum Swartz) is a preferred turfgrass species for golf courses in coastal regions of China. In autumn 2021, patch disease symptoms were observed on seashore paspalum (Paspalum vaginatum Swartz) fairways at several golf courses in Hainan province, China. Fungal isolates with consistent morphological characteristics were recovered from discolored root tissues. Three representative isolates were selected for comprehensive identification based on morphological features and multi-locus phylogenetic analyses. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference of ITS, SSU, LSU, MCM7, RPB1, and TEF1α sequences revealed that the isolates formed a distinct and well-supported clade within the genus Magnaporthiopsis, consistent with their unique morphological traits. Pathogenicity tests demonstrated that the fungus colonizes seashore paspalum roots through ectotrophic dark runner hyphae, casuing to root discoloration, reductions in root and shoot biomass, and leaf chlorosis. Based on morphological, phylogenetic, and pathogenic characteristics, a new species, Magnaporthiopsis paspali, is proposed as the causal agent of root disease in seashore paspalum. In vitro assays showed that propiconazole, benzovindiflupyr, and fluazinam significantly inhibited the mycelial growth of M. paspali, indicating that their potential for effective disease management in field.

title: From People’s War to People’s Rule: Rebel Governance and the Foundations of Inclusive Democracy
affiliations: , London School of Economics, Yale University - Economic Growth Center, , Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar and

detail.title: From People’s War to People’s Rule: Rebel Governance and the Foundations of Inclusive Democracy

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: How does wartime rebel governance shape post-conflict institutions? We study this in Nepal, where the Maoist People's War (1996–2006) dismantled a 240-year caste-based monarchy and ended with Maoists entering democratic politics. During the conflict, Maoists established sub-national "People’s Governments" that administered justice, collected taxes, and delivered local services. Using a spatial regression-discontinuity design, we show that exposure to People's Governments increased political knowledge and participation especially among historically marginalized indigenous groups (Janajatis). Exposure also reshaped party institutions and inter-party competition: candidate-selection committees in more exposed areas have 26 percent more Janajati members who, drawing on novel implicit-attitude data, exhibit less pro-upper caste bias. Non-Maoist parties' Janajati nomination rates nearly double in fully exposed areas, consistent with competition for newly mobilized voters. Nearly two decades on, local governments in exposed areas score 0.2–0.3 standard deviations higher on state capacity indices and receive 13% more in conditional federal grants. These findings show that when rebel groups enter competitive democratic politics, wartime governance institutions can — through citizen mobilization, party gatekeeping, and cross-party competition — enable a more inclusive and capable post-war state.

title: Smart city project impact on regional healthcare expenditure per patient in medium-sized cities: A design-level evaluation of Japan's Digital Rural Health Special Zones
affiliations: Osaka Metropolitan University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Smart city project impact on regional healthcare expenditure per patient in medium-sized cities: A design-level evaluation of Japan's Digital Rural Health Special Zones
detail.abstract: Whether smart-city policy advances urban sustainability depends not on designation alone but on how digital infrastructure is implemented within local service systems. Yet smart-city evaluation has largely treated SCPs as a uniform treatment, leaving the design-level mechanisms through which digital infrastructure produces sustainability outcomes underexplored. This study aims to estimate the impact of SCP implementation on regional healthcare expenditure per patient in medium-sized Japanese cities, using a Bayesian structural time-series design. We examine Kaga and Chino, two medium-sized Japanese cities designated as Digital Rural Health Special Zones in April 2022 under contrasting designs. Using monthly claims-based regional healthcare expenditure (RHE) per patient (April 2018–March 2025) and a Bayesian structural time-series model with 639 non-designated medium-sized cities as donors, we estimated city-specific counterfactuals. As a result, over 36 months, observed expenditure fell below the counterfactual in both cities: -4.9% in Kaga (JPY 24,980; 95% CI: -8.8% to -0.21%; posterior probability 97.6%) and -16% in Chino (JPY 89,978; 95% CI: -23% to -8.7%; posterior probability 99.2%). The cross-city contrast functions as a design-aligned consistency check rather than a statistical test of effect heterogeneity: Chino's earlier and larger divergence is consistent with the theoretically predicted signature of substitutive design, while Kaga's gradual divergence is consistent with the slower, mediated signature of efficiency-enabling design. For sustainable-cities scholarship and practice, the findings support a shift from designation-level to design-level evaluation of smart-city policy and suggest that fiscally productive smart-city investment in aging medium-sized cities depends on whether digital infrastructure targets identifiable urban service bottlenecks.

title: Estimation of Indoor Radon Concentration and Automatic Risk Classification in Multi-Storey Buildings
affiliations: Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Estimation of Indoor Radon Concentration and Automatic Risk Classification in Multi-Storey Buildings
detail.abstract: Radon (222Rn) is a carcinogenic noble gas that accumulates indoors, posing significant public health risks, particularly lung cancer. This study presents a novel conceptual model and algorithm for estimating indoor radon concentration (IRC) in multi-storey buildings by integrating three primary sources: underlying lithology (Ql), active faults (Qf), and building materials (Qb). A porosity-based weighting system (n = 0–1) was developed to account for radon transport through different building elements (floors, walls, ceilings). The algorithm calculates radon concentration at ground floor (Q1 = Ql + Qf + Qb) and first floor (Q2 = Qb), with porosity parameters controlling gas migration. Using a comprehensive dataset of 117 buildings from İzmir, Turkey, the model was validated. Statistical analysis revealed that buildings on alluvium derived from volcanic rocks exhibited the highest IRCs (mean: 210 Bq/m3), with approximately 50% exceeding the European reference level of 200 Bq/m3 (European Commission, 1990; WHO, 2009). Bayesian risk classification categorized 15.3% of structures as high-risk (>300 Bq/m3). Sensitivity analysis identified building material porosity (n1) as the most influential parameter affecting model output. The proposed physics-informed framework offers a cost-effective, interpretable tool for proactive radon risk assessment and mitigation planning.

title:
World Depression 2

A Convergence of Systemic Failures and the Anatomy of an Uncontainable Collapse
affiliations: YuvB Strategic Value Partners

detail.title:
World Depression 2

A Convergence of Systemic Failures and the Anatomy of an Uncontainable Collapse
detail.abstract: This paper advances the hypothesis that the global economy is approaching a structural collapse of a magnitude comparable to, and in several respects more severe than, the Great Depression of 1929. We designate this prospective event World Depression 2, adopting the same retrospective logic by which the Great War became the First World War only after a second emerged. Drawing on current data across fourteen convergent domains, specifically: equity market concentration, artificial intelligence asset inflation, unsustainable AI compute economics (including a documented $1:$20 return ratio and an electricity grid that cannot physically support the buildout), sovereign debt serviceability, dollar reserve erosion, physical precious metals market fracture, systemic volatility signals, interbank funding stress, sovereign bond market deterioration, China's balance sheet recession, commercial real estate maturity stress, zombie corporate debt, the derivatives collateral nexus, and insurance market fracture; this paper argues that these vectors do not operate in isolation. They are mutually reinforcing failure modes simultaneously eliminating the standard policy escape hatches available in 1929 and 2008. Critically, the failure mechanics of the coming crisis will differ from 1929's deflationary spiral: this paper identifies a stagflationary fracture of the global currency order as the operative mechanism, producing comparable or greater severity through different dynamics. In the absence of a synchronised global policy intervention of unprecedented scale and coordination, the structural convergence documented here creates conditions with near-zero margin for error. The paper further identifies the unwinding of the Japanese yen carry trade as the likely transmission mechanism through which latent stress becomes acute crisis, and the $3 trillion private credit market financing AI infrastructure as the structural parallel to the 2007 subprime mortgage market.

title: Priorities in Patronage: Bureaucrat Career Horizons & Targeted Infrastructure in India

detail.title: Priorities in Patronage: Bureaucrat Career Horizons & Targeted Infrastructure in India
detail.abstract: Does bureaucratic ambition shape which local development projects are completed in patronage democracies? Using over 26,000 MPLADS project records from India's 17th Lok Sabha (2019-2024) matched to IAS District Collector career histories and classified by large language models, I examine whether bureaucratic career horizons affect the relative completion of non-programmatic versus broad-based infrastructure. I find that the completion gap between non-programmatic projects-ranging from clientelistic goods directed at named individuals to pork-barrel works concentrated in specific localities-and broad public goods shifts by approximately 33 percentage points across the career horizon spectrum. A one standard deviation increase in years to mandatory retirement-representing a younger, more career-ambitious officer-is associated with an 8.1 percentage point increase in the relative completion probability of non-programmatic projects (β3 = 0.081, p = 0.029). The effect is independent of partisan alignment (p = 0.256) and a pipeline falsification confirms it operates through implementation rather than administrative approval. These findings suggest that bureaucratic career concerns are a structural mechanism sustaining non-programmatic politics in local development-distinct from, and complementary to, accounts emphasizing partisan coordination or initial resource allocation.

detail.abstract: Bitcoin's block reward is scheduled to decline to zero, raising concerns about whether the network can remain secure once miners rely solely on transaction fees. This paper seeks to identify the conditions under which largescale and persistent deviation from honest mining can arise. We analyze and compare the payoffs of honest and deviating miners in a sequential decision model, and identify a deviation threshold Gt at which honest mining ceases to be privately optimal. Around the 2024 Bitcoin halving, we show that current mining behavior does not exhibit large-scale or structural deviation. However, when the block reward is removed, the Gt criterion implies that deviation can arise even with a very small fraction of transaction fees. Finally, we evaluate three protocol-level mechanisms: Base Fee, Fee Floor, and an adaptive maximum block size rule, and show that their combination raises the deviation threshold and mitigates incentive breakdown in a fee-only regime. These results provide a practical benchmark for assessing Bitcoin's security as block rewards disappear.

title: Investment Under Risk and Ambiguity: Insights from Renewable Electricity Production
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management and Industrial Engineering Research Department, CentraleSupélec, Paris-Saclay University

detail.title: Investment Under Risk and Ambiguity: Insights from Renewable Electricity Production
detail.abstract: Investment decisions often face risk and uncertainty. Using the example of the recent evolution of European electricity markets, we show that investors in renewable generation now simultaneously face ambiguous spot prices and a risky production profile. Combining theoretically grounded distributionally robust optimization (to model aversion to ambiguity) and coherent risk measures (to model aversion to risk), we propose a novel tractable formulation of the resulting capacityexpansion problem. We provide an existence result and an economic interpretation of the investment criterion, grounding our proposal in the economic theory of perfectly competitive markets. We then apply our model to the French market case to quantify the relative impacts of risk and ambiguity aversion on investment in onshore wind-generation assets. In so doing, we indicate that ambiguity aversion has a more detrimental impact on investment than risk aversion and urge policymakers to account for ambiguity when they design uncertainty-mitigating schemes to foster investment in renewable generation.

title: The Role of Fractionalization in Estimating the Impact of Economic Shocks on Conflict
affiliations: University of Turin

detail.title: The Role of Fractionalization in Estimating the Impact of Economic Shocks on Conflict
detail.abstract: Assessing the effect of economic growth shocks on the likelihood of civil conflict presents significant obstacles due to endogeneity issues and omitted variable bias. To solve this, I employ exogenous variation in rainfall across Sub-Saharan Africa from 1981 to 2009 as an instrument for economic performance, examining whether the impact on conflict varies systematically with different levels of ethnic, linguistic, and religious fractionalization. I find that while economic shocks alone are weakly predictive of conflict, their effects are significantly amplified in more fractionalized societies. In particular, countries with high religious diversity experience an approximately 7 percentage point increase in conflict likelihood when exposed to adverse rainfall shocks. Reduced-form estimates reveal that ethnic and linguistic diversity are also associated with substantial increases in conflict risk, potentially operating not only through income volatility but via other mechanisms. The findings demonstrate the importance of accounting for social heterogeneity when evaluating the impact of economic shocks on conflict incidence and raise concerns about exclusion restrictions in IV models of conflict.

detail.abstract: Institutional theory's foundational definitions-rules, norms, constraints-describe latent constructs that resist direct measurement in any behavioral record. This article supplies the missing operational vocabulary. Drawing on the classical conditioning paradigm as a universally accessible starting point, it defines seven core analytical primitives: informational signal, perception filter, stimulus, reaction, behavioral pattern, stability, and the behavioral spectrum. These primitives are each anchored to a specific type of observable event-timestamped, agent-tagged, and action-classified-and assembled into a formal definition of a social institution as an empirically distinguishable, statistically stable cluster of behavioral reactions representing one alternative from the spectrum of responses to an identifiable informational signal. The definition carries three mandatory properties-stability, spectral belonging, and signal genesis-and two secondary properties characteristic of mature institutions: autonomization from the original signal and filtering feedback onto new signals. Each concept is first demonstrated in an extended Pavlovian laboratory analogy, then scaled to contemporary human examples including algorithmic governance, tax compliance, and platform-mediated behavior. The result is a conceptual vocabulary that is both empirically verifiable and entirely free of the unobservable essences that have long frustrated institutional analysis.

title: Foreign Exchange Intervention: Identification and Evidence
affiliations: ESSEC Business School - Economics Department

detail.title: Foreign Exchange Intervention: Identification and Evidence
detail.abstract: Foreign exchange intervention is widely used across low, middle and high income economies, yet its effectiveness remains disputed. The central difficulty is identification: interventions are typically endogenous to exchange rate movements, often bundled with other policies and sometimes unobserved. This survey reviews five decades of empirical research and reframes the debate as a problem of causal identification rather than a binary question of whether intervention works. The literature is organized by identification strategy: event studies, reaction-function residuals, controlled regressions, instrumental variables, high-frequency approaches, SVARs, structural portfolio-balance models and natural experiments. For each design, the source of identifying variation and the key assumptions required for causal interpretation are specified. Differences in reported effectiveness largely reflect differences in design, data and regime context. The overall finding is that intervention does affect exchange rates: evidence is strongest for short-run effects on returns and volatility, especially when operations are large, well-timed and implemented in thinner markets. Persistent exchange rate level effects are more sensitive to assumptions about asset substitutability, expectations and financial frictions. The survey provides guidance for empirical practice and highlights priorities for improved measurement and future research.

title: Research Note: Asymmetric Contest Ability in "Agreeing to Lose"

detail.title: Research Note: Asymmetric Contest Ability in "Agreeing to Lose"
detail.abstract: This research note extends the self-signaling model of dispute resolution in McGuire (2026a) to asymmetric conflicts. We model ability asymmetry through exogenous expected contest payoffs, abstracting away from specific conflict technologies. We identify a "Paradox of Strength". A strong agent's higher expected outside option makes them less likely to enter the procedural ritual. However, conditional on entry, their higher opportunity cost renders their participation a more credible self-signal of civic virtue. The strong agent who enters accrues more moral capital from the ritual and holds themselves to a higher moral standard ex post. We also demonstrate that a strength-conditioned reputational look-back decouples the joint equilibrium into independent type-specific subsystems. This preserves the general equilibrium existence and uniqueness identified in McGuire (2026b) and generalizes the result to other conflict technologies.

detail.abstract: On Apr 2, 2025 ("Liberation Day"), the Trump administration announced sweeping tariffs on almost all US trading partners, with rates ranging from 10% to 50%. In response, most major world financial markets dropped. This paper provides a comprehensive look across US stocks, foreign stocks, foreign currencies, commodities, and bonds. US tariffs and Chinese counter-tariffs were about equally important. Many of the most tariff-(and counter-tariff) exposed assets did not decline. Many of the least tariff-exposed assets did. The losses were too large to be explained by tariffs alone. The financial markets thus likely interpreted the harm more broadly as a macroeconomic rather than only a trade-specific shock. Moreover, the actual gainers and losers were likely not who either the US or China had intended.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structure of the euro-area repo market and the role of its key participants, with a focus on primary dealers, drawing on granular data collected under the Securities Financing Transactions Regulation. We document structural features of the market. Outstanding volumes are almost evenly split between centrally cleared and non-centrally cleared segments, which differ markedly in participant composition, maturity structure, and trade characteristics. Within the non-centrally cleared segment – less explored yet systemically relevant – we identify a stable core-periphery network where primary dealers act as central nodes, connecting peripheral entities, such as non-bank financial institutions and non-dealer banks. Primary dealers play a structurally important role in safeguarding the proper market functioning: they channel liquidity from cash-rich agents to those in need of funding, thereby performing a crucial function in the redistribution of liquidity within the system, particularly during phases of reserve rebalancing.

detail.abstract: This article aims to identify and quantify regulations designed to combat poverty, and to assess their effectiveness. Using textual analysis techniques, we systematically classify and quantify, for the first time, all measures adopted in Spain among the 175,204 regulations issued by the Central Administration and the Autonomous Regions between 2007 and 2021. At both levels of government, we distinguish between targeted poverty-related regulations, such as those addressing energy poverty or child poverty, and broader poverty-related regulations, including those focused on precariousness, social assistance, or social exclusion. Furthermore, through multivariate regression analysis, we evaluate whether these regulatory frameworks have had a significant impact on regional risk-of-poverty rates. Our findings indicate that the effectiveness of both targeted and general regulatory measures depends on the level of government responsible for their implementation. Specifically, targeted measures are effective in reducing poverty risk when enacted at the regional level, but not when implemented by the central government. In contrast, broader regulatory measures prove to be effective tools for mitigating poverty when adopted at the national level, rather than by regional authorities. This study contributes to enhancing public sector accountability in Spain and provides valuable insights for refining future policymaking to achieve greater social impact.

title: Stacking the Deck
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Law School, University of Toronto Faculty of Law and University of Virginia School of Law

detail.title: Stacking the Deck
detail.abstract: A federal judicial clerkship is a government-funded Golden Ticket that opens doors otherwise closed to most. This ticket grants entry to a one-year apprenticeship-an exclusive glimpse behind the judiciary's gates that functions as a mentorship-rich fourth year of law school. Historically, a second passage through those gates was exceedingly rare, typically reserved for those en route to the Supreme Court. That norm has fractured. Increasingly, graduates make repeated passes through the gates, taking two, three, or even four clerkships in succession-a practice now known as "stacking." Each additional passage comes at a cost: it reduces the number of clerkship opportunities available to others and delays the clerk's entry into the legal profession. Drawing on roughly 130 interviews with judges, we examine both the rise of stacking and the forces driving it. Our central argument is that stacking is not an irrational pathology but a rational market response to a structural information failure-and that well-intentioned reform efforts have, perversely, made the problem worse. Judges agree that certain forms of stacking are troubling. Yet few see ready solutions. The problem, as they describe it, is not a lack of awareness but a structure of incentives that makes restraint individually irrational, even if the collective outcome is seen as suboptimal. This Essay diagnoses those structural failures and evaluates the most promising paths forward.

detail.abstract: This article critically evaluates the Spectrum Approach as applied in the appellate review of findings of foreign law. The Spectrum Approach posits that the degree of deference to trial judges' determinations of foreign law depends on the analogousness of the foreign legal system to the domestic legal system, situating cases on a spectrum between questions of fact (for dissimilar systems) and questions of law (for closely aligned systems). While the Spectrum Approach attempts to offer a structured framework, this article identifies four key deficiencies with the Approach: (1) over-emphasis on the common-civil law dichotomy, (2) circularity in assessing 'similarity' between legal systems, (3) artificial separation in the ascertainment and application of foreign law, and (4) indeterminacy for cases occupying the middle of the spectrum. This article argues that the Spectrum Approach involves unnecessary inconsistencies and complexities, which the Privy Council did not adequately address in its decision of Perry v Lopag Trust Reg. This article advocates for a flexible, context-sensitive adjudication without any rigid categorisation or sequential reasoning, ensuring consistency with principles of judicial restraint and fairness. This debate has important implications on the treatment of foreign law in domestic courts amid increasing cross-border litigation.

detail.abstract: This paper provides new causal evidence on how patent allowances affect firms and their employees based on quasi-random assignment of patent applications to examiners. Exploiting employer-employee records with newly linked German firm data and web-scraped patent documents, we show that patent-induced shocks reduce firm exit, improve productivity, and increase wages, with rent-sharing elasticities between 0.10 and 0.21. Wage gains are broadly observed across occupational tasks, with substantial heterogeneity: managers benefit disproportionately in publicly traded firms, whereas broader wage increases accrue to workers in non-traded firms. Our findings highlight the role of institutional features and firm organization in shaping how rents are shared.

detail.abstract: Workers sometimes enjoy productive tasks and voluntarily devote unpaid time to them. We study O-ring jobs in which firms can either price a complete task bundle or specify paid task floors while workers remain free to add time. For any allocation supported by both hourly contracts, the wage bill is identical: voluntary top-up is not a discount. The contracts differ because paid floors cannot cap attractive tasks below the worker's voluntary supply. This implementability constraint adds a containment motive for automation alongside replacement and scale effects. It also makes payroll measures incomplete: conditional on a common automated set and a common AI technology, jobs with the same payroll footprint can differ in worked time and task mix. Rich salaried bundle pricing removes the hourly-contract distortion.

affiliations: University of Economics in Bratislava, , University of Technology Sydney (UTS) and Independent

detail.title: Intertemporal Coordination in Volunteer Markets
detail.abstract: Many volunteer markets, and most prominently markets for substances of human origin, feature dynamic coordination problems where volunteering today can temporarily restrict volunteering later. We show that, unsurprisingly, these restrictions reduce market surplus compared to no restrictions. We examine whether providing volunteers with demand or supply information improves market surplus without and with intertemporal restrictions. We show theoretically that, without restrictions, providing demand or supply information increases market surplus, while with restrictions, providing supply rather than demand information causes higher market surplus. Experimental results support most predictions and further show that supply information especially improves market surplus when intertemporal restrictions exist. Overall, comparative static inferences in an environment without intertemporal restrictions do not carry over to an environment with restrictions. Thus, policies based on analyses of static conditions will not necessarily be effective in situations featuring dynamic spillovers.

detail.abstract: This study focuses on retail and e-commerce sector in Oman with an in-depth analysis of Carrefour's competitive advantage over Lulu Hypermarket. The report discusses the role of competition in retail prices and consumer behaviour using key microeconomic concepts like market structure, demand and supply, price elasticity of demand, pricing strategies and government intervention. The study has employed primary sources of secondary data from institutional and corporate sources, such as NCSI, World Bank, IMF, databases of GCC, and company reports, supplemented by price observations of selected food and electronic products. The results indicate that the retail industry in Oman is a monopolistic competitive one in which competition among firms is based on the use of price promotion, product variety, brand and service quality. This is because consumers are extremely price sensitive, as there are close substitutes available and this forces retailers to keep prices competitive and offer promotional discounts regularly. The study also notes the influence of policy, value added tax, consumer protection, import controls, digitalization and consumer attitudes on market outcomes. In general, the report suggests that competition is good for consumers because it drives down prices and increases consumer choice, but also puts pressure on companies to innovate, become more efficient, create better online retailing platforms, and build better customer retention programs.

detail.abstract: Existing prosperity frameworks have significantly advanced development discourse beyond GDP-centric approaches by incorporating wellbeing, sustainability, capability, quality of life, and multidimensional indicators of human flourishing. Yet many of these frameworks remain more effective at describing prosperity conditions and outcomes than explaining the institutional conversion dynamics through which societies translate latent potential into durable developmental progress. This paper introduces “prosperity conversion” as the governance-mediated transformation of latent societal potential into durable, scalable, repeatable, and long-horizon prosperity outcomes. Drawing on prosperity studies, capability theory, institutional economics, governance scholarship, state capability literature, and investment mobilization research, the paper argues that governance coherence, institutional capability, temporal governance capacity, and capital mobilization systems constitute critical but underexamined variables in explaining divergent prosperity trajectories across emerging economies. The paper further introduces the concepts of prosperity conversion capability and prosperity conversion frictions to explain how opportunity, capability, capital, and institutional intent may either compound into durable outcomes or dissipate through fragmentation, discontinuity, weak readiness, and coordination failure. Using Nigeria as a contextual reference point rather than a deterministic case of failure, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for analyzing prosperity conversion systems and outlines implications for research, policy, investment governance, and long-horizon development strategy.

title: From Value Alignment to Moral Operating Systems: The Values and Morale Layer (VML) in Human-AI Symbiotic Architectures

detail.title: From Value Alignment to Moral Operating Systems: The Values and Morale Layer (VML) in Human-AI Symbiotic Architectures
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems evolve from tools into persistent participants in human decision-making, the limitations of existing alignment paradigms become increasingly evident. Current approaches-such as reinforcement learning from human feedback and rule-based frameworks-focus primarily on optimizing outputs, while leaving values implicit, externally defined, and insufficiently governed over time. This paper introduces the Values and Morale Layer (VML) as a system-level architecture for embedding value governance directly into human-AI interaction. VML represents user values as multi-dimensional, uncertainty-aware structures and integrates them into a continuous decision loop that evaluates actions not only in terms of outcomes, but also in terms of value alignment and long-term integrity. Central to this framework is the introduction of morale as a computational variable, operationalized through the Morale Integrity Index (MII), which tracks the longitudinal alignment between values, actions, and experienced outcomes. By combining explicit value representation, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and temporal tracking, VML reframes AI alignment as a problem of moral sovereignty and identity continuity, rather than behavioral approximation. The proposed approach defines a new category of systems-moral operating systems-that support human decision-making while preserving coherence between what individuals value, what they choose, and who they become over time.

This study examines how 22 publicly listed organisations describe their artificial intelligence programmes
in prepared management remarks delivered during earnings calls and, where necessary, in
supplementary public reporting from 2025 and 2026. The coded inventory applies a three-part taxonomy.
Adoption and Containment records statements about usage, deployment scale, cost, efficiency, and
governance coverage. Capability Reporting records measured business outcomes directly attributable to
AI reasoning or synthesis. Product and Marketing Claim records feature descriptions, comparative
claims, and positioning assertions that cannot be verified from outside the firm. Across 22 organisations,
the inventory contains 404 Adoption and Containment statements, 2 Capability Reporting statements,
and 308 Product and Marketing Claims. The ratio is 202 to 1 to 154. Both Capability Reporting

statement meeting the stated threshold. The paper argues that the asymmetry is structural. Enterprise
reporting infrastructure was built for deterministic software, where distribution, usage, and cost were
reasonable proxies for operational effect. The same infrastructure, applied to probabilistic AI systems,
counts use without showing what the model contributed to the work. The study documents a
phenomenon observed in this sample. The finding is not presented as universal.

This paper establishes the epistemological and scientific foundations for corporate Quantum Mechanics and Computational Accounting, providing a radical alternative to the traditional, linear paradigm of management control. Moving beyond the "naive realism" of classical business statistics - which relies on purely epistemic, ex-post probabilities to predict deterministic trajectories - this framework introduces an ontological conception of economic probability. Within the open interval (t0​,t1​), future economic-financial results do not exist as pre-determined figures; instead, they persist as a probabilistic superposition of potential states (potentia) within a corporate Hilbert space. 

By adopting the orthodoxy of the Copenhagen interpretation, this model reframes the Entrepreneur as the definitive measurement apparatus. Strategic intervention and variables definition do not merely forecast a pre-existing market reality, but actively induce the collapse of the system’s wave function, forcing sub-transactional energetic states to localize into tangible economic value. To ground this conceptual architecture into real-world business practice, the paper demonstrates how quantum matrices, phase transitions, and complex probability amplitudes can be mapped directly onto standard relational databases and SQL procedures already in use within enterprise ERP systems. detail.abstract:
The commercial credit score, in its various forms, is fundamentally a payment-behavior aggregator. It records how a business has handled its obligations in the past. It is silent on the question that matters most to operators, lenders, and investors. Whether the business is structurally healthy today, and on what trajectory it sits for tomorrow. Every community lender, fund manager, and equity investor who finances small and medium businesses operates with this gap as a daily constraint. By the time the credit score moves materially, the damage has already happened and the meaningful intervention window has closed.
The Helcyon Score is built to fill that gap. It is an operational health score, not a credit score. It measures the condition of a business from the inside, against that business's own established operating pattern, in real time, with explicit awareness of what is driving any deviation and whether that driver is structural or fixable. The score is diagnostic by construction and prescriptive by extension. It is intended to tell the operator not only where the business stands, but what kind of intervention the score is calling for and on what time horizon.
This paper specifies the methodology behind the score. The five Business Vital Signs, Cash Pulse, Revenue Blood Pressure, Margin Temperature, Customer Heartbeat, and Growth Oxygen, serve as the structural foundation of the framework. Each Vital Sign carries a baseline weight calibrated to its time-to-lethality, and each is modulated by a severity multiplier that depends on the classification of the driver behind any observed deviation. Drivers are classified into five categories. Structural, operational, tactical, cyclical, and strategic. The combination of base deviation, baseline weight, and severity multiplier produces a composite score between zero and one hundred through a weightedaverage normalization. The composite is published alongside a data maturity tier that communicates the engine’s confidence in the underlying baseline as a function of the available data history. The score is read alongside a Recoverability Reading that captures the asymmetry between present operational state and future trajectory, because a poor Cash Pulse signal can reflect either late-stage structural failure or deliberate growth investment, and a strong Cash Pulse signal can reflect either disciplined operation or the harvest of a dying asset. The methodology is designed to distinguish these readings rather than to collapse them into a single number that misleads in either direction.
This paper is presented as a methodology specification at the pre-validation stage of empirical maturity. The methodology is defensible as a diagnostic instrument now, grounded in operational logic and anchored to a published body of theoretical work, but it is not yet empirically validated as a predictive instrument calibrated against observed outcomes in the manner that the FICO score is validated for consumer credit risk. The paper is explicit about that distinction throughout. The path to predictive validation runs through accumulated longitudinal data across the Helcyon customer base over the next three to five years, and the methodology presented here is structured to evolve through that validation rather than be replaced by it.

title: Debt Accumulation, Default, and Relief: Assessing China's Role in Zambia's Sovereign Debt Crisis

detail.title: Debt Accumulation, Default, and Relief: Assessing China's Role in Zambia's Sovereign Debt Crisis
detail.abstract: China's role in African sovereign debt has attracted sustained political and academic attention, yet empirical assessments of its actual contribution to debt accumulation and relief remain scarce. This paper examines Zambia's debt cycle, from its 2020 sovereign default through its restructuring under the G20 Common Framework, through a creditor-by-creditor analysis across four metrics: scale, lending cost, maturity, and annual debt service. The evidence shows that China contributed significantly to Zambia's long-term debt build-up, but the 2020 default was driven primarily by expensive, short-maturity Eurobond obligations. In the restructuring phase, China's participation was necessary to unlock IMF financing and coordinate official creditors, yet its resistance to nominal haircuts and insistence on strict burden-sharing contributed to nearly three years of delays. The overall picture is asymmetric: China bears more responsibility for accumulation than for the default, and was more indispensable than generous in the resolution. Beyond the Zambian case, the analysis exposes structural flaws in the Common Framework, including its income-based eligibility threshold, the absence of a neutral arbiter for Comparability of Treatment disputes, and insufficient disclosure requirements for Chinese loan terms.

This paper presents an exploratory conceptual authentication architecture investigating whether geometric visual traversal patterns, drawn from the Chitrakavi (சித்திரக்கவி) classical Tamil literary tradition, can augment password vault security by adding a spatial-behavioral dimension to key derivation. We frame this explicitly as an exploratory research program, not a finished cryptographic system; all security arguments are bounded by stated assumptions and require empirical and cryptanalytic validation before any deployment consideration.
We propose ChitraVault, a conceptual cryptographic framework that maps the traversal sequences of four canonical Chitrakavi patterns — Chakra Bandha (wheel), Naga Bandha (serpent), Gomutrika (zigzag), and Thiruezhukkootrirukkai (triangle) — onto distinct cryptographic roles within a zeroknowledge password vault architecture. The central contribution is the Visual Pattern Key Derivation Function (VP-KDF), which incorporates a user-drawn geometric pattern alongside a text passphrase and a hardware-bound device fingerprint. The design aims to augment authentication entropy by an estimated additional spatial dimension beyond text-only derivation; precise bit estimates are intentionally avoided, as empirical entropy depends on user behavior distributions not yet measured and theoretical upper bounds derived from path-counting may be substantially optimistic. 
Vault integrity is addressed through a Naga Bandha-inspired chained MAC structure, and key isolation is provided by a Pascal-triangle-shaped hierarchical HKDF key tree. This paper presents formal security definitions (framed as hypotheses pending cryptanalytic review), entropy analysis with explicit independence caveats, pseudocode algorithms, data flow schematics, a comparative analysis against nine existing systems, a structured limitations analysis, and an empirical evaluation plan. 
This exploratory framework is organized around three open research questions: (1) Does a Chitrakavi-inspired pattern gesture provide measurable, statistically independent entropy relative to a text passphrase? (2) Are culturally grounded geometric patterns sufficiently memorable across long intervals to be practical? (3) Does a multi-dimensional authentication surface confer meaningful and durable resistance against realistic phishing and offline brute-force attacks compared to existing multi-factor alternatives? These questions are not answered here — they define the empirical research agenda.

detail.abstract: How do the productivity effects of AI evolve across successive generations of tools, and to what extent do task-level gains ultimately translate into final output? We study these questions in the context of software development, using data on more than 100,000 GitHub developers combined with their AI usage telemetry. In a matched event study design, we find that autocomplete, interactive coding agents, and autonomous coding agents each significantly increase coding activity ("commits"), with respective cumulative effects of 40%, 140%, and 180%. These gains, however, attenuate sharply across the production hierarchy: the 180% cumulative effect falls to 50% for the number of projects, and to 30% for actual releases. This pattern is consistent with the weak-link hypothesis: the strong productivity gains from AI are attenuated by human bottlenecks in the production chain, with an estimated elasticity of substitution of 0.25 between AI and human effort, which indicates strong complementarities. We further confirm these results across four major app marketplaces, finding a moderate increase in the number of new apps but no increase in total usage. Large task-level AI productivity gains have therefore translated only partially into shipped and used software thus far.

title: Why Firm Revenue Appears Heavy-tailed: Evidence from Employment, Composition, and Sectoral Conditioning
affiliations: Idilia Consulting

detail.title: Why Firm Revenue Appears Heavy-tailed: Evidence from Employment, Composition, and Sectoral Conditioning
detail.abstract:
Firm size distributions measured by revenue are frequently reported to exhibit heavy upper tails, in contrast to the markedly thinner tails observed for employment. This observed discrepancy has often been interpreted as evidence for scale-free firm growth. Using firm-level data on publicly listed companies, this paper shows that such interpretations conflate fundamentally different firm populations.
 
Applying rank-based diagnostics and economically meaningful conditioning, we demonstrate that employment distributions are consistently thin-tailed and stable across sectors, regions, and time snapshots. Revenue distributions deviate from Gaussian behaviour only when operating firms are pooled with financial, investment, and real-estate-oriented entities whose revenue is weakly linked to organisational scale. Conditioning on firm type substantially alters the upper-tail behaviour of revenue and restores regular scaling relationships. 

Log-log analyses of revenue versus employment reveal two distinct regimes: near-proportional scaling for operating firms and markedly sub-linear scaling for financial and investment-oriented firms. The coexistence of these regimes explains the apparent heavy tails observed in aggregate revenue distributions. Even in the technology sector-often associated with "superstar" narratives-revenue remains closely tied to organisational scale and does not exhibit Pareto-or Zipf-type tails. 

The results indicate that observed heavy tails in firm revenue arise from population composition rather than intrinsic scale-free growth dynamics.

title: Organisational Values in the AI Era: From Controlled Obligation to Moral Sovereignty in H3LIX OS

detail.title: Organisational Values in the AI Era: From Controlled Obligation to Moral Sovereignty in H3LIX OS
detail.abstract: Organizational values constitute the normative foundation of value-based management, yet contemporary organizations face a persistent and structurally entrenched gap between the values they declare and those they enact. This article examines the core dysfunctions of management by values, including person-organization value incongruence, ethicswashing, deliberate moral manipulation through gaslighting and fake leadership, the absence of longitudinal value tracking, and the oversimplification of moral complexity in organizational decision-making, and argues that existing frameworks remain structurally ill-equipped to govern organizational values under real conditions of uncertainty, power asymmetry, and temporal change. Building on this diagnosis, the article proposes a novel framework for Organizational Identity Integrity Management, operationalized through the H3LIX OS architecture and its Values and Morale Layer (VML). This framework reconceptualizes organizational values as structured, multi-dimensional, and uncertainty-aware computational constructs embedded within continuous organizational decision processes, and introduces organizational morale as a system-level variable reflecting the longitudinal alignment between encoded values, enacted decisions, and organizational outcomes. The article demonstrates how this approach directly addresses each identified dysfunction, enabling a fundamental shift from episodic, compliance-based value governance toward continuous, identity-preserving management of organizational integrity. The findings contribute to the literatures on value-based management, organizational identity, AI governance, and responsible AI, and carry implications for both organizational theory and managerial practice.

Our motivational empirical results show that with greater trade-openness, historically, greater trade deficit led to larger FDI into US. So correcting deficits artificially by a tariff would actually adversely impact FDI flows into US. We then show that:(i) based on the long-run Heckscher-Ohlin [HOS] model where capital is mobile and FDI is an avenue whereby capital outflows could occur based on the rate of return, for US type economy, return to capital will fall as Wage will rise via Stolper-Samuelson effects while for exporting trade-surplus economies like China, the result would be opposite as labor-intensive goods are taxed by US tariff. With sector-specific capital in the exporting trade-surplus economy, return to capital might fall in both places and the result can go either way. detail.abstract: Air traffic controllers often need to decide whether a proposed heading-based clearance remains laterally safe over a finite horizon under uncertain future motion. Nominal straight-line projection is cheap but does not capture bounded speed variation and turn geometry, while richer manoeuvreaware methods are often too costly for repeated filtering or optimisation. We study a pairwise lateral safety test in a local planar model with interval-bounded speeds and at most one fixed-rate turn per aircraft, matching the structure of a single heading clearance. In the straight-heading case, the bounded-speed decision reduces to an exact geometric closest-approach test. In the single-turn case, the fixed-time bounded-speed geometry remains exact and the continuous-time decision is obtained by a certified conservative search in time. On same-model benchmarks, the implementation matched the exact straight-heading result on 100,000 encounters, produced no observed false-safe outcomes on mixed-turn benchmark cases outside the ambiguity band, and kept full turn-aware decisions in the low-microsecond range. Together with an open-source implementation, these results support use as a fast pairwise safety test for evaluating single heading clearances within larger air traffic management, trajectory optimisation, and runtime-assurance workflows.

In consonance with the essence of the New Education Policy, our education governance needs major reforms in order to align itself with the needs of the 21st century. Bulk of this responsibility lies with state governments since they are deeply connected with the educational realities that shape learning outcomes on ground. The case of Bihar presents an opportunity to test these propositions as it is a state having a substantial share of India’s school going population, having resource constraints and visible socio-economic vulnerabilities. 

In line with this, it is the state government, local government, and local institutions of Bihar that have a substantial capacity to streamline educational delivery and outcomes in line with 21st century goals, specifically the New Education Policy. 

This report examined the state of education in Bihar, building on its historical landscape surrounding education and present status. It also identified major laws, key institutions, and policies governing education in the state, with a focus on how the educational laws in Bihar are experienced in practice. Based on the research, the study finds that Bihar’s educational framework is markedly dense yet fragmented with a greater emphasis on input-based regulation and a limited focus on learning outcomes and institutional accountability.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how trade-cost shocks — encompassing freight rates, energy prices, exchange-rate volatility, and tariff regimes — shape apparel import dynamics across luxury and mass-market segments. Drawing on USITC DataWeb import data for HS Chapters 61–62, alongside freight, oil, foreign exchange, and tariff measures, I develop both a theoretical pass-through framework and an empirical panel specification to assess how differently these two segments absorb trade-cost pressure.

The results reveal a meaningful divergence in sensitivity. Mass-market apparel imports contract sharply in response to trade-cost shocks, while luxury imports demonstrate comparative resilience — a pattern attributable to stronger pricing power and lower demand elasticity at the high end of the market. Freight and energy costs emerge as the dominant drivers of import compression. Tariff sensitivity, while currently more muted, appears likely to intensify under the evolving 2025–2026 trade regime.

The paper extends this analysis into equity markets, arguing that trade-cost volatility operates as a systematic factor that redistributes profitability across consumer segments rather than suppressing it uniformly. The implication is structural: luxury firms possess a kind of built-in insulation against supply-chain disruption that mass-market retailers do not. This supports a defensive allocation posture and a long luxury / short mass-market positioning during periods of elevated trade-cost instability.

title: Family Background at Labour-Market Entry: Who Can Afford Early-Career Risk?

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using longitudinal data from the HILDA Survey, this paper examines how socioeconomic disadvantage before labour-market entry shapes early-career labour-market pathways and whether family resources moderate these associations. We model hardship dynamically over ages 4–24 and relate pre-adult trajectories to labour-market risk and precarious-employment pathways over ages 25–30. We identify substantial heterogeneity in both pre-adult hardship and early-adult labour-market experiences, revealing dimensions of inequality that static measures of family background and adult outcomes overlook. Persistent hardship is strongly associated with persistently adverse labour-market trajectories, while moving out of hardship, volatile hardship, and no hardship are linked to substantially lower risks of sustained disadvantage. Family resources partially moderate these associations, but the effects depend on resource type. Short-term insurance provides the clearest buffering role, reducing entry into high-persistent and worsening trajectories. Overall, family resources operate primarily as private insurance against sustained labour-market risk rather than as a mechanism supporting strategic tolerance of precarious work.

title: Explainable Recommendation For Electric Vehicle Charging Stations Considering Range Anxiety And Grid Constraints

detail.title: Explainable Recommendation For Electric Vehicle Charging Stations Considering Range Anxiety And Grid Constraints
detail.abstract: The growing adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) places increasing strain on both individual drivers and the underlying power grid. This paper presents an explainable recommendation framework for EV charging stations that jointly addresses two critical, often conflicting, objectives: alleviating driver range anxiety and respecting grid operational constraints. Leveraging real-time data on battery state of charge, charging station availability, and localized grid load forecasts, the proposed system generates personalized station suggestions accompanied by natural-language explanations. These explanations inform drivers not only of travel distance and estimated waiting times but also of anticipated energy buffer requirements and the grid's current capacity at each location. A key innovation lies in balancing individual utility-minimizing detour and range risk-with system-wide stability, automatically steering users toward less congested stations during peak grid stress. Evaluations using a city-scale mobility simulator show that the explainable recommendations reduce driver-reported range anxiety by 38% compared to baseline proximity-based suggestions, while simultaneously lowering the probability of local grid overload by up to 45%. Furthermore, user studies confirm that transparency regarding both range safety and grid conditions significantly increases driver trust and acceptance of suboptimal but collectively beneficial charging choices.

detail.abstract:
Digital dating platforms have transformed the conditions under which romantic relationships are initiated, shifting interpersonal decision-making from scarcity-based to abundance-based environments. This paper argues that continuous, low-cost exposure to large pools of potential partners amplifies Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) in romantic contexts, increases decision instability, and contributes to relational ambivalence — a state characterised by simultaneous attraction toward and hesitation about commitment. Drawing on the paradox of choice, self-determination theory, attachment theory, and digital wellbeing research, these mechanisms are examined as interconnected rather than discrete processes, and their convergence in the phenomenon of relational ambivalence is traced through the structural and neurocognitive features of contemporary dating platforms.

To integrate these dynamics within a coherent conceptual structure, the paper proposes the DRIVE model — a four-dimensional framework encompassing exposure, impact, regulation, and resilience — as a heuristic and empirically testable scaffold for understanding how individuals engage with, and are shaped by, high-exposure digital relational environments. Implications are discussed for psychological research, clinical and educational practice, digital wellbeing, and platform-level design. The analysis argues that behaviours such as decision instability, commitment avoidance, and ghosting are not reducible to individual psychological deficits, but are in part predictable outcomes of environments engineered to sustain engagement at the expense of relational closure — and that developing adequate theoretical and empirical responses to these conditions represents an important agenda for the psychology of intimate relationships in the digital age.

detail.abstract: The residential renovation market exhibits severe information asymmetry. A homeowner commissioning work cannot reliably judge whether a contractor's quote reflects a fair price for the scale and quality of work actually delivered. This is a textbook lemon market in the sense of Akerlof (1970), and more precisely a credence good in the sense of Darby and Karni (1973) and Dulleck and Kerschbamer (2006): the buyer cannot fully assess quality or necessity even after the work is complete. The result is adverse selection. This paper proposes the Verified Renovation Quote (VRQ) framework, integrating four components: (1) a 170-category reference-price layer — with indicative ranges published openly and precise prices reserved for verification — built on the openly published JCCDB item schema (65,729 items); (2) a contractor-tier margin model that makes scale-appropriate profit ranges explicit rather than hidden; (3) a three-stage verification judgment (approved / conditional / rejected) that refuses to certify quotes lacking internal consistency; and (4) tamper-evident, time-anchored certification, in which a SHA-256 audit hash is committed to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps and issued by an institutionally independent body to preserve neutrality. We describe a working proof-of-concept and the institutional design that makes its certifications credible. We position the contribution as a market-design intervention, not a novel cryptographic primitive. Empirical validation is identified as essential future work.

title: Before Governing the Machine, Govern Ourselves: An Integrity-Driven Framework for People-Centric Leadership Decisions
