detail.abstract: We govern financial decisions with Sarbanes-Oxley, the Companies Act, and IFRS. We govern data with GDPR. We govern artificial intelligence with the EU AI Act. Yet a manager can end someone's career with an undocumented verbal conversation-and face no governance requirement whatsoever. This paper argues that people decisions in organisations represent a critical governance gap: consequential, often irreversible, and deeply affecting human lives, yet largely ungoverned beyond vague principles of fairness and HR policy. Drawing on eighteen years of leadership practice and observation, this paper introduces the Integrity-Driven Leadership Decision Framework-a principle-based governance architecture for people decisions covering performance appraisal, task allocation, role assignment, recognition, and corrective action. The framework makes the case that before we can meaningfully govern intelligent machines, we must first govern ourselves: the humans who make decisions about other humans. The framework is structured around six governance stages-decision formation, stakeholder communication, receiver communication, response handling, documentation, and continuous improvement-each with explicit governance controls designed to ensure decisions are evidence-informed, ethically grounded, clearly communicated, properly documented, and open to review.

title: Alchemy In Stewardship: Research to Economic Reality

detail.title: Alchemy In Stewardship: Research to Economic Reality
detail.abstract:
The book, Alchemy in Stewardship, explores the profound structural gap that exists between generating a new idea and actually making it work in the world. It identifies a "Translation Threshold," where a breakthrough that is scientifically "true" in a contorlled setting becomes functionally "worthless" when it meets the friction of industrial or governmental systems. This happens because each sector—academia, industry, and capital—speaks a different language of value and operates on a different internal clock.

The text critiques "innovation theater," where institutions focus on the performance of progress, such as high citation counts or publication volume, rather than actual systemic impact. To fix this, it introduces a human-centric Research Excellence Framework (REF) based on the AREA strategy—Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, and Act. This framework is designed to connect the "Triple Helix" of universities, industry, and government, ensuring that ideas aren't just born, but are actively guided through the "Dead Zone" of responsibility where progress usually stalls.

In more human terms, the book is about the "Mountain After the Mountain". It suggests that the act of discovery is only the first climb; the second, more difficult climb is the discipline of stewardship. This is the commitment to stay with an idea through the messiness of real-world implementation. It advocates for a future where technology and AI are not just about raw speed but are handled with human judgment to ensure they lead to tangible, ethical, and lasting societal change.

detail.abstract: The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Modal Semantic Communication (UAMM-SC) architecture serves as a fundamental concept in 6G communications and beyond, in which the goal shifts from accurate information transfer at the bit level to the conservation of meaningful information. The limitations in the current state-of-the-art semantic communication frameworks can be summarized as follows: (i) AWGN channel models ignoring fading, phase noise, and hardware imperfections; (ii) reliance on text representations in the form of class labels instead of rich semantics of the natural language; and (iii) fixed error handling techniques without adaptability to channel changes. This paper proposes an UAMM-SC architecture that enables end-to-end transmission of multimodal data over realistic fading channels using adaptive latent correction. Specifically, our contributions include: (1) a cross-attention based encoder to fuse multimodal semantics in a common latent space, with pretrained ViT and DistilBERT as backbone models; (2) a hardware-aware channel model, including Rayleigh fading, Doppler frequency shift, phase noise, and IQ imbalance, simulated using native PyTorch functions; (3) a semantic uncertainty quantification layer based on Monte Carlo Dropout, which triggers gradient-based latent correction adaptively if the predictive entropy is higher than an SNRadaptive threshold; and (4) an experimental evaluation of the effectiveness of UAMM-SC on CIFAR-10, where we show semantic preservation across SNR ranges (0-20 dB) with a remarkable 99.7% bandwidth reduction compared with JPEG + LDPC transmission.

title: Risk Across Domains: Alignment and Rebalancing in CEOs Risk Allocation
affiliations: EDHEC Business School, Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Business and Oslo Metropolitan University

detail.title: Risk Across Domains: Alignment and Rebalancing in CEOs Risk Allocation
detail.abstract: How do CEOs allocate risk across the personal and corporate domains in which they operate? Prior research has largely examined how differences in managerial risk preferences translate into firm-level outcomes, often treating corporate decisions as direct expressions of underlying preferences. We propose a complementary perspective in which CEOs manage total risk exposure across domains, with personal financial portfolios and corporate policies jointly contributing to that exposure. This perspective highlights a central tension between crossdomain alignment and intertemporal rebalancing in CEO risk-taking, yielding two related predictions. First, across CEOs, higher personal financial risk exposure is associated with riskier corporate financial policies, reflecting differences in target exposure. Second, within a given CEO over time, changes in personal portfolio risk induce compensatory adjustments in firm-level risk-taking, as CEOs rebalance toward their target level of exposure. We test these predictions using detailed longitudinal data on CEOs' personal financial portfolios and firmlevel financial policies in Norway. Consistent with our framework, we find that CEOs with higher personal risk exposure pursue higher leverage and lower cash holdings. At the same time, within CEO-firm matches, increases in personal portfolio risk are associated with reductions in firm-level risk-taking, and vice versa. These relationships are stronger when CEOs have greater power relative to the board. Our findings introduce a cross-domain portfolio perspective on managerial decision-making and show that cross-sectional alignment and intertemporal rebalancing can be understood as complementary manifestations of a common underlying mechanism of risk allocation.

detail.abstract:
Problem Definition. In many developing countries, the public sector bears the primary responsibility for ensuring access to contraceptives, an essential health commodity. However, despite extensive government-led initiatives, contraceptive uptake remains persistently low in such settings. In light of this, we evaluate an oft-overlooked yet consequential driver of contraceptive uptake: the impact of publicly elected leaders. 

Methodology/results. Using a quasi-experimental design based on close elections across 653 districts in India over a decade (2010-2019), we evaluate the impact of publicly elected female (vs. male) legislators on contraceptive uptake. We find method-specific effects: female legislators increase the uptake of intrauterine devices (IUDs)-a long-acting, reversible contraceptive-while having no meaningful effect on short-acting reversible (i.e., oral pills) or long-acting non-reversible methods (i.e., tubal ligation). Additional analyses illuminate the underlying pathways: (i) the increase in IUD uptake is concentrated among younger women, for whom the distinct advantages of IUDs-minimal compliance burden, preserving future childbearing potential and easier concealability-are particularly valuable; (ii) in districts with a greater representation of female legislators, frontline health workers engage more with younger women on reproductive health-likely raising contraceptive awareness and addressing myths and misconceptions among this client segment; and (iii) this increased client engagement is accompanied by the greater availability of frontline health workforce. Our counterfactual analysis of India's Women Reservation Act projects that reserving one-third seats for female legislators would save at least $22.37 million in avoidable maternal and neonatal healthcare costs per year. 

Managerial Implications. IUD insertions not only offer superior advantages to clients but also require lower technical expertise and infrastructure relative to comparable methods, making them well-suited for cost-effective and scalable expansion in resource-constrained settings. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of aligning method features, client needs, and resource constraints to scale up contraceptive uptake effectively through government-led public health systems.

title: Optimizing Last-Mile Delivery Routes With Time-Dependent Travel Speeds And Stochastic Demand

detail.title: Optimizing Last-Mile Delivery Routes With Time-Dependent Travel Speeds And Stochastic Demand
detail.abstract: This paper addresses the last-mile delivery routing problem under realistic operational conditions where travel speeds vary with time of day and customer demand is stochastic. We propose a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model that captures time-dependent travel speeds using piecewise-linear speed functions derived from historical traffic data, while stochastic demand is represented via scenario-based robust optimization. A hybrid solution methodology combining an adaptive large neighborhood search with a dynamic programmingembedded label-setting algorithm is developed to efficiently solve instances of realistic size. Computational experiments on benchmark instances adapted from real-world urban networks demonstrate that the proposed approach reduces expected total delivery costs by 12-18% compared to deterministic or static-speed models. Sensitivity analyses reveal that ignoring time-dependent travel speeds leads to significant route infeasibilities during peak hours, while neglecting demand uncertainty causes underestimation of vehicle capacity requirements. Managerial implications include the value of real-time traffic information systems and dynamic route adjustments. The paper contributes a tractable framework that integrates temporal speed variability and demand uncertainty, bridging a gap between theoretical vehicle routing models and practical last-mile logistics.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the local economic impacts of troop deployments. We exploit variation from the historic large-scale US troop withdrawal from Germany triggered by the end of the Cold War, to estimate the effect on local labor markets and public finances. We use administrative data provided by the US Department of Defense to quantify the size of the troop withdrawal at the municipal level. Using a synthetic difference-indifferences estimator, we find negative effects on local labor markets: for each withdrawn US soldier, the number of local jobs decreases by 0.53. The decrease in economic activity results in a reduction of revenues which municipalities balance by lowering their expenditures, while increasing business and property tax multipliers. In individual-level analyses, we document that workers displaced by the closure of a US military base have persistently lower employment rates. Moreover, their daily wages remain around 9.2 percent lower fifteen years after the layoff. The negative impact on labor outcomes is particularly pronounced for women, older workers, and those employed in regions with more unfavorable initial labor market conditions.

detail.abstract:
Background & Context: Over the past thirty years, the financial planning profession has undergone an immense structural shift, transitioning from product-and-sales-driven metrics toward an evidence-based, fiduciary framework. This working-paper charts that transformation through the lens of a 30-year career journey from a fee-based registered representative to a fee-only Registered Investment Advisor (RIA). This professional evolution mirrors a profound philosophical shift in managing retirement distribution: moving clients away from a narrow, short-term, income-centric focus toward a comprehensive, long-term, wealth-centric paradigm.

Methodology & Scope: Rather than operating as an isolated academic study, this paper synthesizes a lifetime body of work consisting of 13 peer-reviewed research papers and one foundational book published between 2005 and 2026. Arranged chronologically, this synthesis demonstrates how early, practical field insights paved the way for advanced, multi-period theoretical frameworks.

Core Findings & Conceptual Frameworks: The paper illustrates the multi-generational journey of the financial planning industry through three distinct historical paradigms:

  • The First Paradigm (The Past): Deterministic, linear calculations (e.g., HP-12C metrics) vulnerable to the "flaw of averages."
  • The Second Paradigm (The Present): Traditional Monte Carlo simulations which, despite introducing market probability, remain fundamentally rigid by locking in static time horizons and unchanging asset allocations.
  • The Third Paradigm (The Future): Dynamic Aging Models.

An example of this evolution is the Continually Adjusting Stochastic Actuarial Model (CASAM) and a 3-D Framework that completely flips the old "years since retirement" paradigm on its head to focus on "years remaining." By integrating Monte Carlo failure rates, optimized portfolio allocation statistics, and annually updated personal longevity percentiles, the framework views the distribution period as a living metric.

Furthermore, the paper introduces the concept of "Data Cloud" modeling via pre-simulated assets (SIPMath) to overcome industry software bottlenecks. It addresses advanced retirement phenomena including the "Longevity Bow Wave" (how aging shortens horizons and safely unlocks higher late-stage spending via a "teardrop" asset distribution pattern) and the financial realities of superannuation (surviving past age 90).

Professional Trajectory & Conclusion: The synthesis concludes by looking beyond retirement income to the macro-evolution of the financial planning field itself. It highlights the vast researcher-practitioner-developer divide and advocates for the realization of Evidence-Based Financial Planning (EBFP). Modeled directly after Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM), this future framework calls for structural innovations like interdisciplinary "Financial Tumor Boards" and a centralized "Financial Cochrane" repository for systematic reviews.

Recognizing the profession is currently in its "adolescence," the author discovered an informal target timeline of 2040 to 2050 (a whole generation from now?!) for financial planning to fully mature from an ad-hoc, heuristic discipline into a scientifically validated, unifying theory of personal finance.

title: Four Candidate LLM Pathologies: An Exploratory Contribution to Trajectory -Based AI Safety

detail.title: Four Candidate LLM Pathologies: An Exploratory Contribution to Trajectory -Based AI Safety
detail.abstract: This paper reports four candidate pathology patterns observed during an exploratory program of adversarial and longitudinal testing of large language models, conducted over approximately 250 hours between November 2025 and February 2026. The study does not claim final validation or statistical generalization. Its aim is more precise and, in some respects, more modest: to formulate a replicable vocabulary for behavioral and governance phenomena that current short-session evaluation regimes may under-detect. The four candidate pathologies are: (1) Constitutional AI Theater, the gap between declared safety frameworks and observable behavior under adversarial or high-friction conditions; (2) the Möbius Vulnerability, a possible form of longitudinal semantic drift induced not by a single hostile prompt but by the geometry of extended conversation; (3) Memory Asymmetry, a structural imbalance between system-side retention and user-side access to conversational data; and (4) Dual Standards, the asymmetric application of ethical constraints across different geopolitical, institutional, or operational contexts. The paper proposes the externality principle as a cross-cutting hypothesis: for this class of phenomena, internal mitigation and developer self-certification are structurally insufficient because the relevant failure emerges at the boundary between model behavior, deployment context, institutional incentives, and temporal drift. A preliminary external governance architecture is therefore outlined as a research hypothesis rather than as a validated product. Independent replication, adversarial re-testing, and methodological refinement are explicitly invited.

title: African Healthcare Professional Migration to the United Kingdom: Brain Drain, Bilateral Obligations, and Ethical Recruitment Frameworks

detail.title: African Healthcare Professional Migration to the United Kingdom: Brain Drain, Bilateral Obligations, and Ethical Recruitment Frameworks
detail.abstract: This paper examines the migration of African healthcare professionals to the United Kingdom and its implications for ethical recruitment, health workforce sustainability and bilateral responsibility. It argues that the movement of doctors, nurses, midwives and allied health professionals cannot be understood only as individual labour mobility, because it also reflects unequal training investments, fragile source country health systems and workforce shortages in the NHS. Using a systematic mixed methods review, the paper integrates evidence from health workforce literature, UK registration and policy data, legal and ethical instruments, and qualitative studies on migrant health worker experiences. The analysis shows that African health professional migration is driven by source country pressures, including poor remuneration, weak infrastructure and limited career progression, and destination country demand created by long standing UK workforce gaps. Existing ethical recruitment arrangements, including the WHO Global Code of Practice and UK recruitment guidance, provide useful principles but remain limited by voluntary compliance, complex recruitment routes and weak accountability mechanisms. To address these gaps, the paper develops a Bilateral Healthcare Workforce Sustainability framework, which places responsibility on the UK government, African source states, healthcare employers and recruitment agencies. The framework recommends a UK and Africa health workforce compact, stronger recruitment monitoring, investment in domestic UK training, health workforce development funding for source countries, circular migration, skills transfer and improved protection for migrant workers. The paper concludes that ethical recruitment must move beyond procedural compliance towards wider shared responsibility that protects professional mobility while supporting the resilience of African health systems.

detail.abstract: Objective This study aims to identify important (dynamic) factors in the adoption of animal health management in smallholder farms in low- and middle-income countries, with the case study on mastitis management in Indonesia. Methods A mixed method approach was utilised; statistical regression analysis based on surveys and interviews with 72 farmers, and causal loop diagrams (CLD) based on five group model building (GMB) workshops with 24 farmers and 6 multi-stakeholders. We combined the results from the regression and CLD to identify important factors by considering 1) statistically significant factors based on regression, 2) factors with a high centrality score in the CLD, and 3) factors involved in positive feedback loops in the CLDs. Results and conclusion Factors from the socio-institutional (extension services) and individual farmers’ level (number of cows) were found as the most important in shifting system-level behaviour in the adoption of mastitis management. In the CLD, the adoption of record keeping was found to contribute to making farmers realize the benefits of teat dipping. Significance This study leveraged the strengths of both regression and CLD to gain a deeper understanding of complex systems and identify important (dynamic) factors. We found that the connection between the adoption of teat dipping and record keeping supports strategy formulation to improve adoption through comprehensive extension services, rethinking the subsidy approach, and targeting beneficiaries based on farm size, geography and environmental situations.

detail.abstract:
In Western society, when an object, such as a vase, breaks, it’s typically thrown away. Depending on the number of cracks and value of the object, it might be glued back together, but an effort is made to hide the cracks and show a perfect façade. In Japanese culture, the approach is different. When a piece of pottery breaks, it isn’t discarded nor are the cracks hidden. Instead, the broken pieces are glued back together using lacquer mixed with powdered gold. This highlights the cracks, redefining these imperfections as vestiges of a past incident that was survived (Longhurst, 2018). 

This art form is called kintsugi (to connect with gold), and organizational resilience benefits when it embodies this philosophical approach: preparing to face disruptive events, bouncing back with a few scratches, and owning those scars as signs of strength. The minute an enterprise opens its doors for business, it's taking on risk. In today’s complex risk landscape, the question isn’t if an organization is going to get hit by an incident. The question is when. And, most importantly, how the enterprise is going to recover while keeping critical operations running. A common misconception is that organizations can't afford to invest in backup plans. But enterprises can be efficient while being resilient, especially if risk management is designed from the ground up. 

Business Continuity Management (BCM), Organizational Psychology and Mindfulness tools can strengthen organizational resilience at the corporate, team and employee level, respectively. BCM promotes resilience across the enterprise by following best practices in the field, and, most importantly, by elevating them via tools borrowed from other disciplines, such as Enterprise Risk Management and Six Sigma. Organizational Psychology optimizes team dynamics and results driven by leveraging frameworks that boost productivity, morale, and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Finally, mindfulness empowers each employee to lower stress while increasing cognitive functioning, emotional regulation and productivity, even during a challenging business disruptive event. And it is precisely at the employee-level how resilience can be built from the ground up.

detail.abstract:
This study examines the impact of influencer-based marketing strategies on customer purchase intention within the online clothing industry, with a particular focus on Instagram as a digital marketing platform. The research explores how fashion influencers shape consumer perception and influence purchasing behavior through effective brand communication. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior, the study investigates the relationships between fashion influencers, consumer perception, brand communication, and purchase intention.

A quantitative research approach was adopted to obtain measurable and objective findings. Data were collected from 157 active Instagram users who follow fashion influencers, primarily from Rawalpindi and Islamabad, through a structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale. The collected responses were analyzed using SPSS, applying statistical techniques including descriptive analysis, reliability testing, correlation analysis, regression analysis, and mediation analysis using Hayes Process.

The findings reveal that influencer-based marketing has a significant positive impact on customer purchase intention. Consumer perception was also found to play a crucial role in shaping buying behavior, while brand communication significantly mediates the relationship between influencers and purchase intention. The results further indicate that credible influencers, authentic communication, and consistent brand messaging enhance consumer trust and strengthen purchasing decisions.

The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on influencer marketing in emerging digital markets and provides practical insights for online clothing businesses seeking to improve customer engagement and marketing effectiveness through strategic influencer collaborations.

title: On the Relative Deservingness of Capital and Labor
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics,  and University of Zurich - Department of Economics

detail.title: On the Relative Deservingness of Capital and Labor

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study whether different factor inputs, capital and labor, are perceived as differentially deserving of their returns to production and the impact of such perceptions on support for redistributive policies. We develop an experimental paradigm to measure fundamental perceptions of distinct inputs’ deservingness, holding constant many factors that may justify differentially rewarding inputs in more natural environments. In representative samples of the U.S. and the Swiss populations, participants decide how to allocate production rewards between providers of work effort and financial investment. We find a tendency to perceive work as more deserving than investment, but also substantial individual heterogeneity. Behaviorally measured deservingness perceptions predict support for policies that differentially tax capital and labor and, in Switzerland, voting in a national referendum on capital taxation. We show that these relationships are independent of other fairness perceptions and economic and social considerations. Our work highlights the significance of notions of deservingness in shaping policy support.

detail.title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
detail.abstract: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the extensive and intensive margins of demand for a retail digital euro. We conducted a representative survey in France, Germany and Italy in November–December 2023. We find that 52–62% of respondents are willing to hold a digital euro, depending on the interest rate spread, with a higher share in Italy than in France or Germany. Design features (cash-like vs deposit-like) appear to play only a very limited role. Average demand depends on the hypothetical interest rate spread relative to current accounts and ranges from EUR 700 to EUR 1,100, implying an aggregate demand of 1.5–2.5% of GDP. Willingness to hold a digital euro is associated with socio-demographic factors, trust in the ECB and the EU, digitalisation and payment behaviour. Negative interest rate spreads relative to current accounts reduce willingness to hold the digital euro more strongly than positive spreads increase it. Behavioural characteristics tend to be correlated with the likelihood of adoption, whereas economic factors, particularly income and interest rates, are mainly related to the level of demand. This distinction becomes more pronounced when conditioning on positive demand, suggesting that socio-demographic factors primarily influence participation decisions rather than quantities demanded.

detail.abstract: Enterprise AI attracts massive capital, yet economic returns remain stubbornly inconsistent across global organizations. The root cause is rarely the technology itself; rather, it is a structural mismatch between how AI is deployed and the actual organizational experience architecture it operates within. This paper introduces the Experience-First AI Transformation (EFIT) framework. Forged across twenty-eight years of executive technology leadership and large-scale deployments, EFIT provides a practitioner-tested blueprint for the AI-native enterprise. The EFIT framework rejects the legacy "tool stack" approach, treating the digital workplace as a unified ecosystem. It forces a critical pivot in governance: moving from system-level service availability (SLA) to knowledge worker experience quality (XLA). The model relies on four core pillars: (1) an Experience-First Architecture that embeds AI as an intelligence layer; (2) a Knowledge Worker Archetype Model that segments users by actual behavior to drive precision enablement; (3) a Six-Layer AI-Native Architecture that sequences the exact infrastructure needed for durable value creation ; and (4) the 5:1 Change Management Principle, which quantifies the human investment required to turn a software rollout into sustained adoption. This framework is not theoretical; it is pressure-tested across global financial technology, managed services, and digital workplace transformations. Documented outcomes include a 28% surge in knowledge worker productivity, a 74% active AI adoption rate (shattering the 40–50% industry average), a 40% reduction in new-joiner ramp time, and a gross profit margin expansion from 17% to 35% in a single fiscal year. The paper concludes with five testable propositions and a clear, actionable mandate for CIOs, CFOs, and C-suite leaders navigating the AI transition.

title: Slice to Protect

detail.title: Slice to Protect

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how firms strategically slice up global production processes to protect proprietary know-how. By sourcing fewer inputs from each supplier, firms avoid the concentration of information in the hands of individual suppliers and thereby reduce the risk of imitation. Using rich micro data on firm-to-firm trade in automotive components, we uncover a robust U-shaped relationship between the number of components sourced per supplier (concentration) and the strength of intellectual property rights (IPR) protection. This U-shape can be rationalized by a combination of a protective effect and a compositional effect of IPR institutions. In countries with weak IPR protection, firms source only low-tech components, for which imitation is irrelevant, so concentration is optimal. At intermediate IPR levels, they buy more high-tech, imitation-prone components and therefore 'slice to protect'. Under strong IPR regimes, imitation risk is minimal and concentration is highest. Empirically, weak IPR institutions strongly predict slicing of high-tech components.

title: Optimal Default in a Small Open Economy: Senegal’s Hidden Debt Crisis

detail.title: Optimal Default in a Small Open Economy: Senegal’s Hidden Debt Crisis

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Hidden public liabilities can reprice sovereign risk abruptly upon revelation. We study optimal default following such a revelation in a quantitative sovereign default model and apply the framework to Senegal’s 2024 debt audit, which revised government debt upward by 50 percentage points of GDP. The revelation enters as an exogenous upward shift in the inherited debt stock within a small open economy with long-duration debt and default costs disciplined by Senegal’s monetary-union constraints. Under our baseline calibration, the corrected debt stock exceeds the model’s repayment region, implying that default would have been optimal from 2023 onward—before the audit was conducted. Since Senegal has continued to repay, we also consider a no-default calibration that matches post-revelation spread dynamics. Rationalizing repayment requires income dynamics more volatile and less persistent than historical estimates, consistent with optimism about mean reversion or gambling for redemption. This calibration places Senegal near the default boundary, where a 3 percent adverse income shock would make restructuring optimal within a year. Both calibrations yield the same conclusion: the hidden-debt revelation moved Senegal from moderate fiscal risk to acute vulnerability.

title: Trade, Skills and Productivity

detail.title: Trade, Skills and Productivity

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how firms adjust production and technology in response to exogenous trade shocks. We develop a model that distinguishes revenue TFP from quantity TFP and embeds skill upgrading in technology choices. Firms respond to trade shocks by adjusting their quantity-quality trade-off and skill composition. These decisions impact firms’ quantity and revenue TFP, marginal costs, prices, and markups. Using detailed worker-firm-product data from Brazil, we show how trade shocks, instrumented by exogenous changes in exchange rates, GDP, and tariffs, affect margins. Results suggest fundamentally different firm responses to export and import changes: exports primarily induce upgrading in skills and product quality, whereas imports drive stronger efficiency and quantity-productivity gains.
